chapters.title: Chapter 1131. We March to Excise the Cancer
paragraphs: The great field outside Aethelgard’s southern gate had never witnessed such a terrifying display of concentrated power. The morning air was cold, tasting of frost and the sharp tang of impending violence.
Thousands upon thousands of soldiers stretched across the plains like a living tide of steel, arranged in flawless, deadly formations.
Banners bearing the ancient sigils of a dozen noble houses snapped and cracked in the biting wind, their colors vivid against the gray sky.

At the vanguard stood the combined ranks of the Apostle network disciplined, silent, and unnerving, while behind them, the elite household forces and conscripted levies formed a vast, bristling forest of spears and pikes.

At the center of this assembled storm stood a massive wooden platform, elevated high above the sea of armor. Three figures stood atop it, silhouetted against the pale dawn, waiting for the moment the world would change.
Valentina occupied the center position. She stood like a monument carved from marble, her posture radiating a calm, unshakeable authority that commanded respect without needing to demand it.

To her right stood Apollo, his face a mask of grim solemnity; he carried the expression of a man who had already weighed the lives of thousands against the survival of the city and found the bargain necessary.

To Valentina’s left stood the Avatar. It was a perfect, uncanny mirror of Rex Rexilion, the same measured confidence, the same predatory stillness, and the same way the light caught the sharp angles of its face.

But beneath that flawless exterior, the true consciousness that animated it sat hundreds of meters below their boots, ensconced in a throne room drenched in violet-black shadows, coiled like a serpent waiting for the signal to strike.
Valentina raised a single hand. The effect was instantaneous.
The low murmur of thousands of voices didn’t fade; it died. A wave of absolute silence swept outward from the platform, rolling across the field until even the wind seemed to hold its breath.
"We stand here today," Valentina began.

Her voice didn’t need to scream; it carried across the vast expanse of the field through a seamless blend of natural projection and subtle magical amplification that made her words feel as though they were being whispered directly into every soldier’s ear.
"We stand here because this city has absorbed more grief over these past months than any civilization should be asked to bear."
"We have not just fought wars; we have endured nightmares."
She paused, her gaze sweeping over the assembled faces, some young and eager, others old and hollow-eyed with exhaustion.
"We have buried our brothers in unmarked graves."
"We have watched innocent children age backward through horrific forces none of us fully comprehend."
"We have watched our people torn apart by a corruption that should never have been allowed to touch our soil."

"We lost one of our own, a lion among men, to a darkness that crawled up from beneath our very feet." Her jaw tightened almost imperceptibly at the memory. "And in our darkest hours, we have questioned whether Aethelgard’s foundations were strong enough to withstand the rot that continues to gnaw at our bones from below."

The silence that followed was heavy, suffocating, charged with the collective trauma of a city pushed to its breaking point. Rex, watching from the periphery, felt the tension in the air vibrate like a plucked string.
He could almost smell it: the metallic copper of future blood, the sulfur of magical discharge, the sweat of terrified men about to become legends.
Valentina’s eyes flashed with a cold, righteous fire. "Today is not merely a military campaign."
"Today is not a simple march to reclaim territory." Her voice rose, gaining a resonant power that seemed to make the ground tremble. "Today, Aethelgard reclaims control over its own fate!"

"We march not out of vengeance alone, though vengeance has its rightful place in every honest heart standing here, but out of the simple, brutal, and necessary conviction that no city can call itself safe while a threat this persistent, this vile, continues to operate beneath its own foundations unchallenged!"
She leaned forward slightly, her presence expanding to fill the entire field. "We do not march to negotiate!"
"We do not march to contain!"
"We march to excise the cancer!"
"We march to tear the throat out of the darkness and remind the world beneath us that Aethelgard does not fear the shadows; we hunt them!"

As Valentina stepped back, the space she vacated seemed to pulse with residual authority. Apollo moved forward, stepping to the very edge of the platform as if daring the approaching storm to meet him halfway. He didn’t just speak; he resonated.
His life affinity bled into his words, creating a harmonic frequency that bypassed the ears and struck directly at the solar plexus.

When he opened his mouth, his voice didn’t travel through the air; it saturated it. It was a warm, living thing that wrapped around every soldier on that field, making the distant levies feel as though he were standing mere inches from them, speaking directly to their souls.
But beneath that warmth lay something molten and dangerous.
"We remember," Apollo began, and the word itself felt like a vow. "We remember those who cannot speak for themselves anymore."
His gaze swept across the formation, sharp enough to pierce armor.

"We remember Veylor." The name hung in the air like a funeral dirge. "A soldier who fought with honor, a partner who deserved a lifetime of peace, stolen from Iris before their story could even truly begin."
"We remember the hollow ache left behind in those who loved him."
A low, guttural murmur rippled through the ranks. Apollo didn’t pause; he drove forward, twisting the knife of shared grief to forge it into a weapon.
"We remember Calivara and Eryndra..."

"Women who stood as pillars of our strength, who shared our purpose and our blood for years, only to be butchered in a single, cowardly ambush that defied every rule of engagement we hold sacred." His jaw clenched, the tendons in his neck standing out like iron cables. "They didn’t fall in a fair fight..."
"They were slaughtered."
The anger in the crowd began to simmer, visible in the way hands tightened on sword hilts and shields creaked under increased pressure.

"And we remember the children." Apollo’s voice softened, taking on a haunting, almost reverent quality that made the hair on the back of Rex’s neck stand up. "The children of the outer districts who bore witness to horrors that should only exist in nightmares!"
"Children whose very lifelines were twisted aged backward by a corruption that mocks the natural order of life itself!"
"What kind of monster feeds on the stolen time of the innocent?!
The question was rhetorical, but the fury it provoked was physical. The air seemed to grow heavier, charged with a static tension that tasted like copper.
Then, Apollo’s expression shifted. The righteous anger cooled into something more complex, something darker and more intimate.

"And we remember Theo." His voice dropped to a dangerous register, thick with a complicated sorrow that made the crowd lean in, spellbound. "We lost him not to an enemy blade, but to the rot from within!"

"We lost him to a corruption that turned brother against brother, friend against friend." He paused, letting the grim reality sink in. "We will not condemn him with simple hatred, for we know the cruelty of the infection that claimed him!"
"But we will honor his memory by ensuring that no one else ever has to suffer that same betrayal of their own flesh."

A few murmurs of surprised approval broke through the silence. Those who had expected a simple speech of condemnation found something far more potent: a recognition of the terrifying, messy reality of their war.

Apollo straightened his spine, his entire presence suddenly expanding as his life affinity flared, casting an almost luminous glow around him. "Today marks the last day the Underlayer is permitted to threaten the peace we’ve fought so hard to maintain!"
"Today, we stop reacting!"
"Today, we stop mourning!"
"Today, we huuuuuuunt...!"
The climax of his words acted as a spark dropped into a powder keg.
The response was not merely a cheer; it was an explosion. A thunderous, earth-shaking roar erupted from thousands of throats, a primal scream for vengeance that seemed to bruise the sky.
Simultaneously, thousands of soldiers slammed their spear butts against the packed earth in perfect, terrifying unison.
THOOM. THOOM. THOOM.

The sound was physical. It was a wall of noise that shook the wooden platform beneath Apollo’s feet and sent vibrations through the very bones of everyone present. The ground itself seemed to tremble in submission to the collective rage of the army.
In that moment, the field wasn’t just a gathering place; it was a forge, and the soldiers were the steel, being hammered into a single, unstoppable weapon of war.
As the thunderous reverberations of Apollo’s speech began to settle into a tense, vibrating silence, the Avatar stepped forward. The shift in energy was immediate and visceral.

If Apollo had been the heartbeat of the army, the Avatar was its mirror, a symbol of impossible heroism that had become the city’s living myth. A hungry curiosity rippled through the ranks as thousands of eyes fixed on the figure who bore Rex Rexilion’s face.
The Avatar did not speak with the booming authority of a general or the divine resonance of an Apostle.
Instead, it adopted a register of quiet, measured humility, the voice of a soldier who had bled in the same trenches as every man and woman standing in the mud.
It was a performance of perfect empathy, calibrated to make the crowd feel not like subjects being commanded, but like comrades being understood.
"We have counted the names," the Avatar began, its voice carrying that uncanny, steady calm that felt like a blade cutting through the morning fog. "We have written them in our hearts."
Then, it began to speak. One by one, it named the fallen.

chapters.title: Chapter 1132. They Think They Come to Excise a Cancer, They Are Walking Into the Furnace
paragraphs: "Kaelen... Mara... Silas..." The Avatar allowed each name to hang in the air like a physical weight, forcing the soldiers to confront the emptiness each loss left behind. "Each one a brother... Each one a sister..."
"Each one a piece of the foundation we stand upon." The pauses were surgical, allowing the grief to breathe, to sting, to transform from raw pain into something sharper: resolve.

"I know what some of you whisper in the dark when the torches burn low," the Avatar continued, its gaze dropping slightly, as if sharing a private confidence with the masses. "You wonder if we are enough..."
"You wonder if a single city can truly hold back the tide of something so ancient, so hungry."

The Avatar looked up, its eyes Rex’s eyes scanning the formations with a calculated warmth that felt almost achingly genuine. "I know many of you have wondered why Helena Von Starlight isn’t standing here with us today."
A murmur of recognition swept through the crowd. "She remains on her mission with Leonidas, far from our walls."
"Every one of us knows she would be at the front if she could... But let me tell you this: her absence is not a crack in our armor."
"It is our greatest strength."
It stepped closer to the edge of the platform, its presence seeming to expand. "Aethelgard has never been defined by a single hero."
"We have never relied on one person to carry the sky on their shoulders."

"We stand here today with Helena, with Leonidas, with every legend you can name because we have proven that the city’s true strength lives in the person standing to your left and the person standing to your right."
"We stand because you choose to stand."
A ripple of fierce, prideful emotion stirred the ranks. The Avatar seized the moment, its voice building with the inexorable momentum of a gathering storm.
"Our chances are not merely hopeful; they are absolute."
"We carry a key forged with the genius of our finest scholars, a weapon of precision designed to pierce the heart of darkness."
"We carry Apollo, whose very life force will light our path through the deepest abyss."
"We carry Valentina’s ironclad promise that not a single innocent soul will pay the price for this crusade."
The Avatar’s face hardened, the mask of humility slipping to reveal something far more primal: the face of a predator ready to feast. "And most importantly, we carry you..."
"The bravest assembly of warriors this world has ever seen."
"The Underlayer has taken our homes... They have taken our children.
"They have taken our dead." Its voice dropped to a low, dangerous growl that vibrated in the chests of every soldier present. "Today, we take back everything they stole."
"Today, we hunt."
The field didn’t just erupt; it detonated.

Thousands of swords, spears, and halberds rose in a single, unified salute that blotted out the morning sun. The roar that followed was a physical force, a tsunami of sound that rolled across the plains and slammed against the ancient stone walls of Aethelgard like a battering ram.
On the platform, Valentina, Apollo, and the Avatar exchanged a final, silent look—a shared understanding of the deception, the danger, and the inevitable carnage to come.
The performance was complete.
The trap was set.
"March!" the command finally tore through the air.
The disciplined cacophony began as the formations shifted. The massive army began its organized, inexorable advance toward the underground gateway where the Key awaited.

Thousands of boots struck the earth in a rhythmic, deadly cadence as disciplined columns of steel moved toward the mouth of the underworld, marching with grim purpose and righteous fury directly into the jaws of a slaughter they believed would be their salvation.
Far beneath the floating majesty of Aethelgard, the world was stripped of light and replaced by something far more sinister.

The northern corridor stretched like a diseased throat through solid rock, a narrow, claustrophobic passage that felt less like a tunnel and more like the digestive tract of some ancient, subterranean god.

Veins of natural crystal threaded through the stone walls, pulsing with a sickly, arrhythmic glow, a dim, shifting luminescence that cast elongated, dancing shadows that seemed to writhe independently of their sources.
This was not merely a passage; it was a kill box.

Thousands of Underlayer soldiers stood in absolute, terrifying silence. They were arranged in meticulous, overlapping layers of defensive formations, each tier positioned with surgical precision according to Gorvasha’s complex geological calculations.

This wasn’t a random gathering of warriors; it was a trap designed with the patience of a spider. The air here was thick, tasting of mineral dust, cold stone, and the metallic tang of sharpened steel.
Every man and woman present knew they were the teeth of a trap that had been years in the making, waiting for the moment the surface world would finally expose its throat.
Cassandra stood at the precipice of this assembled storm. Having just concluded the final tactical briefing, her voice still seemed to echo off the crystal-veined walls.

The authority she wielded was not the performative bravado of a general, but something far more primal: the residual, bone-deep command of a former Demon Queen. When she spoke, the soldiers didn’t just listen; they obeyed as if her words were physical laws.

She had walked through every gruesome detail one last time, her mind a cold map of impending slaughter. She knew the exact millisecond the rear guard would seal the corridor’s exit, cutting off any hope of retreat.

She had calculated the precise delay required to lure Aethelgard’s initial wave deep enough into the throat of the corridor before the true engagement began long enough for the trap to snap shut with bone-crushing force.
The rotation schedules were flawless; no gap would form, no weakness would emerge, no matter how many bodies piled up in the dark.
’Let them come,’ she thought, her inner voice as cold as the stone beneath her boots. ’Let them march with their righteous fury and their hollow promises.’
’They think they come to excise a cancer, but they are merely walking into the furnace.’
A sudden distortion in the air near her shoulder shattered the stillness. The light didn’t just bend; it tore.
A high-tier teleportation shimmer coalesced into the imposing, masked silhouette of Lord Xerollion. The effect on the assembled forces was instantaneous and terrifying.
Thousands of warriors moved as one, boots striking the stone in a synchronized, formal salute that reverberated through the corridor like a single, thunderous heartbeat.
Cassandra turned to face him, her spine straightening with instinctive deference, though her eyes remained sharp with tactical satisfaction.
"Everything is in position," she reported, her voice steady, devoid of hesitation. "The formations are set like iron teeth."
"The rear guard has been briefed on the exact timing of the seal; there will be no escape once the first blade is drawn."
"Every commander down the line understands their role in this symphony of death; they know precisely when to hold, when to push, and when to grind them into the dust."
She paused, her gaze sweeping over the endless rows of weapons glinting in the sickly crystal light. "We have calculated every variable, Lord Xerollion."
"The trap is sprung; we simply await your hand to release the mechanism."
Rex gave a single, curt nod. Even beneath the inscrutable stillness of his mask, there was an unmistakable aura of predatory satisfaction.

He began to speak, his voice dropping into a low murmur as he offered a series of surgical refinements to the plan: minute adjustments to timing, a three-second delay in the third tier’s advance, and a slight shift in the spear wall angle to better funnel the Aethelgard cavalry into the kill zone.

These were not mere suggestions; they were the final touches on a masterpiece of slaughter, informed by the intimate intelligence he had absorbed while wearing the Avatar’s face at the surface gathering.
His gaze drifted down the endless corridor, finding Gorvasha standing several hundred yards back among the secondary formations. Their eyes met in a silent exchange.

Gorvasha offered a single, imperceptible nod, a cold, mathematical confirmation that the geological calculations remained flawless. The stone would hold; the corridor would not collapse prematurely; the ambush would be as precise as a guillotine blade.

As the assembled commanders dispersed to their respective positions, their armored boots echoing like hammer blows against the stone, a fragile window of stillness opened before the inevitable storm. Rex did not use this time for prayer or meditation.
Instead, he moved through the ranks with the fluid, deliberate grace of a panther, seeking out the women who occupied the most dangerous and vital positions within his war machine.
He found Cassandra first. She remained at the absolute vanguard, a statue of dark resolve amidst a sea of steel.

Rex approached her without ceremony, stopping close enough to feel the heat radiating from her body. He reached out, his gauntleted fingers surprisingly gentle as he hooked two fingers beneath her chin, tilting her face upward to study her features in the sickly crystal light.

chapters.title: Chapter 1133. The Air Here Tastes of Too Much Death Already
paragraphs: "Your strategic instincts have grown considerably sharper since the day I first met you," Rex said, his voice carrying a rare note of genuine appreciation. "Back when you were less concerned with grand design and more focused on trying to put a fist through my mask."
Cassandra didn’t flinch. Instead, her lips curved into a dry, dangerous smile, the kind that had once made lesser demons flee in terror.
"Don’t sound so surprised, Xerollion... I was the finest general Mordecai ever commanded."
"I learned how to read a battlefield long before you came along to dismantle his empire and claim everything he held dear."

Her tone carried its familiar sardonic edge, but as she looked up at him, the fire in her eyes softened into something more complex, something almost vulnerable. "Still... some days, it feels surreal."
"The Demon Queen, who once drew blood simply by speaking her name, is now standing here in the dark, waiting for a mortal man’s signal like any other soldier."
Rex leaned closer, his breath ghosts against her cheek. "You aren’t waiting for a signal like any other soldier, Cassandra."
"You aren’t a pawn on this board... You built half of this trap yourself."
A flash of genuine pride ignited in her expression, replacing the melancholy. "I suppose that’s true."

She allowed herself one more heartbeat to savor the acknowledgment, letting the moment of connection linger before the cold reality of the coming massacre rushed back in. Her features hardened instantly, the Demon Queen reasserting control as she pulled away from his touch.
"But pride won’t kill Aethelgard. Only blood will."
The brief personal respite vanished as quickly as it had appeared, folded away behind walls of discipline and steel.
Rex left Cassandra to her cold vigilance and moved deeper into the pulsing throat of the corridor. His next stop was Gorvasha.

The air around her felt heavier, charged with the raw, geological energy she commanded. Standing beside her, Rex offered praise that lacked Cassandra’s sardonic bite; there was no teasing here, only the direct, sincere acknowledgment of a predator recognizing another’s perfect kill strike.
He spoke of the structural integrity of the kill zones and the flawless channeling of the ambush and the tactical brilliance of turning solid stone into a weapon.

Gorvasha accepted the words not with a smile, but with the grim pride of her people. She thumped a closed fist once against her own sternum, a dull, hollow sound that echoed like a funeral drum against the crystal walls.

"This corridor will be remembered in the songs of the deep," Gorvasha said, her voice carrying that characteristic low growl that seemed to vibrate the very stone beneath their feet. "Not as a passage, but as a tomb."
"This is where Aethelgard’s arrogance finally meets its limit... where their bones will become part of our foundation."
"I will not let you down, Lord Xerollion."

Rex offered her a final moment of recognition, his hand resting briefly against her armored shoulder, a gesture of solid, unshakable trust, before continuing his journey through the deadly architecture of the Underlayer.
The further he moved, the more the atmosphere shifted. The air grew humid, slick, and strangely sweet-smelling.

He was approaching the contingent commanded by Viscaria. As he drew near, he saw her slime kin soldiers, translucent, undulating masses of lethal protoplasm shifting restlessly, their forms rippling in unconscious sympathy with their mistress’s emotions.
Viscaria herself was a vision of fluid danger, but as Rex approached, her usual composure fractured. Her form shifted subtly, her surface tension wavering with visible unease.
"You’ll be careful," Viscaria said, skipping any pretense of formality.

The words came out raw, almost desperate. Her hand drifted instinctively, almost protectively, to the visible, swollen curve of her belly, the life growing within her a fragile miracle amidst a sea of impending slaughter.
"I know your reputation..."
"I know you have walked through hells more vicious than this and emerged unscathed."
"But I still worry. The air here... it tastes of too much death already.
Rex didn’t offer empty platitudes. He knew she needed truth, not comfort.
He stepped into her space, closing the distance until the heat of her shifting form pressed against his armor. He reached out, resting his palm gently against the swell of her stomach.
Beneath his touch, he could feel the faint, miraculous warmth of her life force a stark contrast to the cold, mineral death surrounding them.
"I always come back," Rex promised, his voice dropping to a private murmur that barely carried past her.
His thumb traced a slow circle over her skin. "I have survived everything the world has thrown at me because I have something worth returning to."
"I return for you, Viscaria... And I return for the future we are carving out of this darkness together."

For a moment, the war, the trap, and the thousands of soldiers waiting to spill blood faded into the background. There was only the heartbeat of the woman before him and the silent vow of the man who would burn the world to protect it.

Rex made his final circuit through the labyrinthine kill zone, the oppressive atmosphere of the corridor growing heavier with every step. The air seemed to thicken, saturated with the unspoken promise of violence.
His last stop took him to a shadowed alcove tucked away at the corridor’s jagged edge, a vantage point that offered a perfect, unobstructed view of the surface reserve forces.
There, shrouded in the darkness like a living ghost, waited Lilith.

She barely had time to register his presence before she was moving, throwing her arms around him with a desperate, fierce affection that nearly knocked the wind from his lungs. Her embrace was a lifeline, a reminder of humanity in a place designed for annihilation.
"You never have time for me anymore," she whispered against his chest, her voice carrying that familiar dramatic flair she used as both armor and weapon.

But beneath the theatrical complaint, Rex could hear the genuine ache of it—the fear of a woman who knew exactly how easily a man could be swallowed by war. "Everyone else gets their precious moment of connection before this stupid war starts."
"I get shoved into this godforsaken corner to babysit a reserve force that probably won’t even be worth the effort of killing."

chapters.title: Chapter 1134. Move Forth and Claim What Is Ours by Divine Right
paragraphs: Rex let out a breath he hadn’t realized he was holding, unable to suppress the ghost of a smile that her theatrics always managed to coax from his guarded heart. He wrapped his arms around her, holding her against the cold metal of his armor.
"Your ’corner’ happens to be the most critical watch post in this entire operation, Lilith," he said, his voice dropping to a low, intimate murmur. "Without your eyes, the entire flank collapses."

"You aren’t a spectator; you’re the guardian of our rear." He pulled back just enough to meet her eyes, his gaze unblinking beneath the mask. "And I promise you this: once the blood has dried and the last of Aethelgard’s fools has been buried, you’ll have more of my time than you know what to do with."
"I will make good on that vow."
Lilith searched his masked face for a long moment, her lips parting as if to speak, before she finally released him. "I’ll hold you to an absurd amount of time, Master."

"Don’t think you can escape that debt." Before she retreated back into the shadows, she pressed one last, searing kiss to his jaw, a fleeting spark of warmth that stood in stark, almost painful contrast to the gathering storm of steel and hatred surrounding them.
Rex turned away, the levity fading as quickly as it had come. He began the long walk back toward the center of the formation, each footfall echoing with the finality of a death knell.
The minutes were no longer ticking away; they were bleeding out.
He took his position at the absolute heart of the assembled Underlayer forces, a throne of shadow and steel. From this vantage point, he could see the entire scope of his design.

The northern corridor stretched out before him like an elongated throat, waiting to be fed. Somewhere beyond the sealed stone ahead, the gateway to the surface world waited to vomit forth Aethelgard’s finest: their shining armor, their righteous fury, and their precious lives, all of it destined to be ground into crimson paste against the unyielding stone.

Beneath the mask, Rex’s expression settled into something terrifyingly calm. It was the stillness of a predator who had already won, the unshakeable certainty of a man who had spent months calculating every variable, every angle of attack, every bone that would snap, and every throat that would be slit.
Every woman he loved, every commander he had forged into a weapon, and every soldier he had placed like a chess piece—they were all exactly where they needed to be.
The machinery of death was fully assembled. The gears were greased with anticipation.
Now, there remained nothing left to do but wait for the first scream to echo through the tunnel, signaling that the trap had finally sprung.

Deep beneath the western wing of the Grand Academy, in a chamber that had been sealed behind layers of sanctified wards for weeks, the air had grown stale, charged with a static that made the hair on the back of every soldier’s neck stand on end.

This was not merely a room; it was a pressure cooker of divine ambition. The assembled forces of Aethelgard filled the cavernous hall from wall to wall, a sea of polished steel, gleaming white armor, and the righteous fury of a nation poised to strike.
At the epicenter of this contained storm stood Elizabeth. She looked smaller than intended against the backdrop of the gathered armies, but the power she wielded made her appear monolithic.
She stood within the intricate confines of an elaborate ritual circle etched into the ancient stone, her fingers white-knuckled around the key.

The artifact hummed in her grasp, its golden light pulsing in a slow, deliberate rhythm, a heartbeat that seemed to synchronize with the collective, anxious breathing of the thousands gathered to witness its activation.
Behind her, the hierarchy of Aethelgard stood in disciplined, terrifying silence. Apollo and Valentina occupied the vanguard, their presence as immovable as mountains alongside the Avatar.
Behind them stretched endless rows of Apostles and elite shock troops, their weapons gleaming in the magical glow, their eyes fixed forward with a zealotry that bordered on madness.

The tension in the space was physical; it felt as though the very atmosphere had been compressed, pressing against the stone walls as if the chamber itself might burst from the sheer weight of expectation.
Elizabeth began.
Her movements were not those of a frightened girl but of a scholar who had rehearsed this symphony of destruction countless times in the lonely hours of her research.

Her hands began to weave the dual simultaneous grimoire pattern, a technique so complex, so demanding of mental and spiritual fortitude, that lesser mages would have suffered brain hemorrhages attempting it.
Her fingers danced through the air, leaving trails of residual mana that shimmered like liquid fire.
The Key responded with terrifying immediacy. Its golden pulse quickened, transforming from a heartbeat into a frantic staccato.
The light intensified, shifting from a warm glow to a searing, blinding radiance that threatened to burn through retinas. Then, the chamber began to scream.

It started as a faint tremor, a low growl from the bowels of the earth. Then came the cracks—fine, spiderwebbing fractures of golden light that erupted from the ritual circle, spreading outward like the roots of some primordial, celestial tree tearing through solid rock.
The stone groaned in protest, ancient mortar crumbling as the magical pressure reached critical mass.
"Hold the formation!" Apollo’s voice rang out, a thunderclap that cut through the rising cacophony of grinding stone. "Steady yourselves!"
"The goddess commands the path!"

The tremor escalated into a violent convulsion. Dust and debris rained from the ceiling as the light reached an unbearable crescendo, forcing the Apostles to shield their eyes behind armored gauntlets.
Then came the climax: a single, overwhelming explosion of pure dimensional energy that didn’t just crack the wall but seemed to shatter the very concept of space.

A sound like a thousand glass cathedrals shattering simultaneously echoed through the chamber. When the searing white flash finally receded, leaving spots dancing in everyone’s vision, the far wall was gone.

In its place stood a massive dimensional gateway, a yawning maw of swirling energy that defied human comprehension. It was far larger than Elizabeth’s calculations had predicted, a gaping wound in reality wide enough for entire phalanxes to march through side by side.
The space beyond shimmered with a disorienting, kaleidoscopic quality, the distorted light of the Underlayer bleeding through the threshold like ink in water.
A ripple of awestruck silence moved through the ranks. Younger Apostles stared, their mouths agape at the raw, unbridled scale of the magic.
This wasn’t just a portal; it was a violation of natural law.
Valentina gave a single, sharp nod, her composed features betraying nothing but a cold, calculating satisfaction. She had wanted this power, and now it stood before them, raw and bleeding.
Apollo did not wait for the awe to fade. He stepped forward, the clank of his greaves cutting through the ringing silence like a blade.
His voice rolled across the chamber with the absolute authority of a man who knew that hesitation was the only sin left to commit.
"Apostles! Soldiers of Aethelgard!" Apollo roared, his sword catching the sickly light of the gateway. "The path is open!"
"The gods have granted us the throat of the enemy!"
"Move forth and claim what is ours by divine right!"
"MAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAARRRRCCCCCH!"

He wrapped his arms around her, holding her against the cold metal of his armor.
"Your ’corner’ happens to be the most critical watch post in this entire operation, Lilith," he said, his voice dropping to a low, intimate murmur.
"Without your eyes, the entire flank collapses."
"You aren’t a spectator; you’re the guardian of our rear." He pulled back just enough to meet her eyes, his gaze unblinking beneath the mask.
"And I promise you this: once the blood has dried and the last of Aethelgard’s fools has been buried, you’ll have more of my time than you know what to do with."
"I will make good on that vow."
Lilith searched his masked face for a long moment, her lips parting as if to speak, before she finally released him.
"I’ll hold you to an absurd amount of time, Master."

"Don’t think you can escape that debt." Before she retreated back into the shadows, she pressed one last, searing kiss to his jaw, a fleeting spark of warmth that stood in stark, almost painful contrast to the gathering storm of steel and hatred surrounding them.

Every woman he loved, every commander he had forged into a weapon, and every soldier he had placed like a chess piece—they were all exactly where they needed to be.
The machinery of death was fully assembled.
The gears were greased with anticipation.
Now, there remained nothing left to do but wait for the first scream to echo through the tunnel, signaling that the trap had finally sprung.

The assembled forces of Aethelgard filled the cavernous hall from wall to wall, a sea of polished steel, gleaming white armor, and the righteous fury of a nation poised to strike.

She looked smaller than intended against the backdrop of the gathered armies, but the power she wielded made her appear monolithic.

Behind them stretched endless rows of Apostles and elite shock troops, their weapons gleaming in the magical glow, their eyes fixed forward with a zealotry that bordered on madness.

The tension in the space was physical; it felt as though the very atmosphere had been compressed, pressing against the stone walls as if the chamber itself might burst from the sheer weight of expectation.
Elizabeth began.
Her movements were not those of a frightened girl but of a scholar who had rehearsed this symphony of destruction countless times in the lonely hours of her research.

Her fingers danced through the air, leaving trails of residual mana that shimmered like liquid fire.
The Key responded with terrifying immediacy.

Then, the chamber began to scream.

chapters.title: Chapter 1135. The Final Heartbeat Before the Slaughter
paragraphs: "Forward! March!" Apollo’s command tore through the chamber like a battle cry, and the disciplined machine of Aethelgard began to grind into motion.

The formations shifted with terrifying synchronization. Apollo himself plunged through the shimmering veil of the gateway first, his cape swirling behind him as he led the primary assault force into the unknown.
Valentina followed with the cold precision of a predator, her division positioning themselves to secure the retreat corridor, a necessary precaution that she treated as a tactical inevitability.
At the rear, Morwenna’s elite Nightwing soldiers fell into formation like shadows coalescing, their dark armor swallowing what little light remained.

The Avatar moved through the central ranks like an avenging god, its face a mask of serene, inhuman resolve, while Elizabeth stumbled slightly as she joined the procession, her breathing ragged, the golden light in her hands fading to a dull, exhausted ember now that the impossible task of tearing open reality was complete.
The transition through the gateway was not a simple walk; it was a violation of the senses. For each soldier, those few seconds felt like an eternity spent drowning in liquid gold.

The air became impossibly dense, pressing against their lungs until they gasped for breath, their vision consumed by a kaleidoscopic distortion that made their own hands look alien. Then, with the suddenness of a blade’s strike, the light vanished.
They plunged into the thick, cool darkness of the Underlayer.
The disorientation was immediate. One moment they were bathed in divine radiance; the next, they were stumbling through a claustrophobic throat of stone.
The only light came from the faint, sickly pulse of natural crystals embedded in the walls, casting long, dancing shadows that seemed to writhe with malevolent intent.
The sound was overwhelming the thunderous, echoing rhythm of thousands of armored boots striking stone, a metallic heartbeat that reverberated off the narrow walls.
Apollo emerged at the head of the column, his sword drawn and glowing with a faint holy light. He scanned the northern corridor, his eyes narrowing as he took in its grim architecture.

For a heartbeat, a flicker of tactical satisfaction crossed his face. The corridor was perfect, a flawless funnel that would channel their overwhelming numbers directly into the enemy’s heart. It was exactly what an invading force needed.
But as the last of his vanguard passed through the threshold, that satisfaction curdled into something cold and poisonous.
"Something is wrong," Apollo whispered to himself, though his words were drowned out by the clatter of marching steel. "Too quiet..."
"This shouldn’t be this... quiet."

The silence of the Underlayer wasn’t the absence of sound; it was an active, hungry thing. It pressed against their ears like water. There was no echo of enemy patrols, no distant sounds of mining, and no skittering of vermin, just the rhythmic, deafening march of Aethelgard’s boots.
It felt like walking into the gullet of a beast that had already swallowed and was now simply waiting for the next course to pass through its teeth.
’It’s a trap,’ a voice screamed in the back of Apollo’s mind, but he suppressed it. ’No, we have the numbers... We have Rex.’
’We have the Apostles.’
’We will crush whatever waits in the dark.’
The unease spread through the ranks like a plague. Soldiers glanced at one another, their eyes darting toward the shadows where the crystal light failed to reach.
The air felt wrong too—still, too heavy, as if the oxygen itself had been replaced by something thicker, something that tasted faintly of old blood and cold metal.
Apollo felt the hair on his neck bristle. His instincts, honed through decades of holy warfare, were screaming at him.
The silence wasn’t peaceful; it was the silence of a held breath. The silence of a predator mid-leap.
"HALT!" Apollo roared, thrusting his fist upward. "Form defensive squares!"
"Tighten the files! Eyes on the flanks!"
The column began to slow, the thunderous marching breaking into the confused scraping of armor and boots trying to find purchase on the stone.
But the warning was a heartbeat too late. The trap didn’t just spring; it exploded.
The silence didn’t break; it shattered.

From the impenetrable darkness at the far end of the corridor, something began to manifest. At first, it was merely the suggestion of movement, pale reflections off steel, and the faint scrape of leather on stone.
Then, the shapes coalesced. A handful of figures emerged, then dozens, then hundreds, then thousands.
They didn’t stumble from the shadows; they materialized from them in perfect, terrifying synchronization.
Underlayer soldiers stepped forward as one, a wall of disciplined steel and obsidian armor that seemed to absorb the dim crystal light rather than reflect it.
Their weapons—long spears, serrated cleavers, and heavy maces—were held at precise angles, creating a forest of deadly metal. There was no chaos here.
No panicked shouts. No disorganized rabble.
This was a machine of war, polished and oiled, waiting for the signal to grind its teeth.

A visible ripple of terror tore through Aethelgard’s front ranks. The confidence that had carried them through the gateway—the righteous certainty of divine conquest—evaporated like mist in a furnace.
These weren’t the scattered insurgents they had been promised; these were professionals who had been waiting for them.
"Gods above..." one young Apostle whispered, his voice cracking as he gripped his sword with white knuckles. "They knew... They were waiting for us."
Apollo didn’t answer. His jaw was set so tight it felt as though his teeth might crack.

His entire body was coiled like a spring, every nerve ending screaming warnings of imminent annihilation. His gaze swept across the opposing wall of death, searching for a weakness, a gap, a single flaw in their flawless formation.

But there was none. The Underlayer formation was a masterpiece of tactical positioning, a defensive structure so complete and so deliberate that it felt less like an army and more like a trap that had been set months ago.
Then, Apollo saw him.
At the dead center of the opposing mass, the crowd of soldiers seemed to part instinctively, creating a focal point of absolute stillness.

Flanked by the terrifyingly poised figures of Cassandra and Gorvasha, a single masked figure stood motionless. Even across the stretch of the narrow stone passage, the aura radiating from the masked commander was suffocating.
It wasn’t just authority; it was a cold, predatory calm that seemed to drain the heat from the air.
’Someone is...’ Apollo’s inner voice hissed, a cold dread settling in his gut. ’Someone orchestrated this...’
’Every step we took, every breath we drew since the gateway opened... it was all... his design.’

The two armies faced each other like two tectonic plates grinding against one another, the pressure between them building to an impossible degree. The air itself seemed to hold its breath, suspended in that horrific, agonizing moment before a storm breaks.
Neither side moved. Neither side blinked. Thousands of eyes locked onto thousands of others, righteous fury meeting cold, calculated annihilation.

The silence stretched, taut as a bowstring pulled to the point of snapping. Then, from somewhere deep within the Underlayer ranks, came the first sound: the metallic click of a shield locking into place.
Then another. Then the low, guttural scrape of swords being drawn from scabbards.
The sound rippled outward through the formations like a wave of impending doom.
It was the prelude. The final heartbeat before the slaughter began.
Both sides understood now that this was not a battle for territory or glory; it was a collision of fates that would leave nothing but blood and broken bones in its wake.

chapters.title: Chapter 1136. Cities Bury People, It’s One of the Few Things They’re Designed For
paragraphs: The silence in the northern corridor stretched beyond the point of discomfort, warping into something grotesque and unnatural. Thousands of soldiers stood frozen, trapped in a tableau of impending slaughter.

The pale blue light bleeding from the crystal seams washed over the assembled armies, casting sickly shadows across their faces and transforming every tense jawline and widened eye into something inhuman and monstrous.

In that unbearable quiet, sensory details became hyperfocused: the rhythmic, maddening drip... drip... drip of water echoing from some unseen cavern far behind them; the metallic tang of oiled steel; the sour stench of unwashed bodies and adrenaline-soaked leather; the smell of wet stone that seemed to cling to the back of the throat.
Each heartbeat felt like a hammer blow against the eardrums.
Apollo Brightsoul finally broke the spell.
He didn’t shout. He didn’t charge.

Instead, he stepped forward from the vanguard of Aethelgard’s formation. His boots rang against the stone with three deliberate, measured paces that carried him away from the safety of his phalanx and into the exposed killing ground between the two armies.
His hands were held slightly away from his sides, not in surrender, but in the practiced, controlled gesture of a commander seeking parole before unleashing hell.
Valentina followed a heartbeat later. Her movements were serpentine and controlled, the faint shimmer of active defensive wards still clinging to her shoulders like a ghostly second skin.

Neither of them spared a glance at the thousands of lives hanging in the balance behind them. Their focus was singular, locked entirely on the masked figure at the heart of the Underlayer’s obsidian wall.

Flanking that figure were Cassandra and Gorvasha, standing like twin pillars of inevitable death, while Mordecai Vrael hovered half a step behind them, looking conspicuously out of place, a disgraced power seeking purchase in a new world order.
Apollo studied the masked commander with the clinical intensity of a predator cataloguing a rival.

For months, the name Lord Xerollion had been a ghost in the Apostle intelligence reports, a whispered myth of a man who had seized control of the Underlayer with impossible speed, restructuring its entire power dynamic before anyone could even realize the throne had changed hands.
The reports had called him a demon, a tyrant, and a god. But the reality standing before Apollo was far more unsettling.
The figure wasn’t a hulking brute like Gorvasha; he was built lean, corded with wiry muscle that suggested explosive speed rather than raw crushing power.
The mask covering the upper half of his face was deceptively simple, plain, unadorned, and utterly devoid of emotion. It didn’t scream menace; it refused to acknowledge it.
’What kind of man stands like that?’ Apollo wondered, his grip tightening imperceptibly on the hilt of his sword. ’No fidgeting... No shifting of weight... No nervous breath...’
’He isn’t bracing for a fight; he’s waiting for an inevitability.’
The stillness was absolute. Xerollion hadn’t moved an inch since the two armies had locked eyes. He stood as though he were carved from the very stone of the corridor itself.

Behind that mask, Apollo felt a gaze unreadable, ancient, and terrifyingly patient sweeping over him and Valentina. It was the look of a man who had already seen every possible outcome of this confrontation and found them all wanting.

The air between them grew colder, charged with a static that made the skin crawl. The two most powerful figures Aethelgard could muster and stood in the mouth of the lion’s den, facing a man who didn’t seem to fear death because he seemed to own it.
"So you’re the one who’s been hiding beneath our city all this time," Apollo said finally.
His voice broke the tension not with a shout, but with the controlled power of a man who commanded the very essence of life.

His life affinity lent his words a resonant, harmonic quality that carried effortlessly through the narrow passage, vibrating against the stone walls until even the soldiers at the very rear of both formations could hear his challenge.
"Lord Xerollion... We finally meet face to face."
"Apollo Brightsoul."
The response came from behind the mask, but it wasn’t the voice of the man they knew as Rex. This voice was lower, a gravelly register that seemed to vibrate from the floorboards of the world itself.
It was deliberately weighted, pitched to carry menace rather than any semblance of human warmth. "Your reputation reached me long before you did..."
"The songs of your bravery precede you."
"They tell me you lead this force with great courage, which I suppose is one way of describing how far you’ve marched into territory that was never yours."
Apollo’s eyes flashed with holy fire. "This territory sits beneath a city that has buried more of its own over the past several months than it did in the previous twenty years combined."
"We’ve seen the bodies, Xerollion... We’ve seen the aftermath."
"Cities bury people, Brightsoul," Xerollion replied, his tone conversational, almost bored. "It’s one of the few things they are actually designed for."
A sharp intake of breath hissed through the Aethelgard ranks. Valentina stepped forward half a pace, her boots clicking like a death knell against the stone.
Unlike Apollo’s measured diplomacy, her voice was a blade cold, accusatory, and honed by months of grief.

"Let’s not pretend this is some philosophical debate about urban planning," Valentina snapped, her eyes blazing with the fury of a woman who had watched her students die in terror. "There is a figure who calls himself The Undead Bringer, who has butchered apostles in their own beds, in places where our wards should have made them untouchable.
"There is an entity called Tremor who leveled our northern district, turning stone to powder and civilians to meat in a single afternoon."
"There is a half-dragon operative who nearly burned Aethelgard to its foundations."
"Every thread of every investigation, every drop of blood we’ve scraped off our streets, leads down here."
"Into your territory... Into structures you control."
She took another step, her hand hovering near the hilt of her weapon. "So I am going to ask you directly, in front of both our armies..."
"How much of that was the Underlayer’s doing?"

The question hung in the air like a guillotine blade suspended by a thread. For several agonizing seconds, the only sound was the distant dripping of water and the ragged breathing of thousands of terrified men.
During that pause, Xerollion’s head turned. It was a miniscule movement, barely an inch, toward Mordecai Vrael standing behind him.
It was too subtle for the soldiers to read, but to Apollo, it felt like a silent accusation. ’Is he looking at his accomplice? Or is he reminding him of his debt?’

"The Underlayer is not a single hand, Valentina," Xerollion said at last, his voice cutting through the tension like a scalpel. "It is two hundred thousand souls living in a dimensional layer that your city has treated as a garbage pit for eight centuries."
"You dump your sins here and expect them not to fester."
He took a single step forward, and the Underlayer soldiers behind him shifted in unison, their armor clanking with the sound of approaching doom. "Things move in the dark."
"Some of them move with my knowledge."
"Some of them move simply because the filth and corruption your people created made their movement inevitable."
"If you want me to stand here and confess to the specific authorship of every catastrophe that has ’inconvenienced’ Aethelgard, you’ll be disappointed."

His masked head tilted slightly, the dim crystal light catching the edge of his visor. "But if you want me to deny that the Underlayer has been involved in your recent suffering, you’ll be lying to yourself."
"And I have absolutely no interest in helping you maintain your delusions."

Their focus was singular, locked entirely on the masked figure at the heart of the Underlayer’s obsidian wall.

Flanking that figure were Cassandra and Gorvasha, standing like twin pillars of inevitable death, while Mordecai Vrael hovered half a step behind them, looking conspicuously out of place, a disgraced power seeking purchase in a new world order.
Apollo studied the masked commander with the clinical intensity of a predator cataloguing a rival.

For months, the name Lord Xerollion had been a ghost in the Apostle intelligence reports, a whispered myth of a man who had seized control of the Underlayer with impossible speed, restructuring its entire power dynamic before anyone could even realize the throne had changed hands.
The reports had called him a demon, a tyrant, and a god.
But the reality standing before Apollo was far more unsettling.
The figure wasn’t a hulking brute like Gorvasha; he was built lean, corded with wiry muscle that suggested explosive speed rather than raw crushing power.
The mask covering the upper half of his face was deceptively simple, plain, unadorned, and utterly devoid of emotion.
It didn’t scream menace; it refused to acknowledge it.
’What kind of man stands like that?’ Apollo wondered, his grip tightening imperceptibly on the hilt of his sword. ’No fidgeting...
No shifting of weight...
No nervous breath...’
’He isn’t bracing for a fight; he’s waiting for an inevitability.’
The stillness was absolute.
Xerollion hadn’t moved an inch since the two armies had locked eyes.
He stood as though he were carved from the very stone of the corridor itself.
Behind that mask, Apollo felt a gaze unreadable, ancient, and terrifyingly patient sweeping over him and Valentina.
It was the look of a man who had already seen every possible outcome of this confrontation and found them all wanting.
The air between them grew colder, charged with a static that made the skin crawl.
The two most powerful figures Aethelgard could muster and stood in the mouth of the lion’s den, facing a man who didn’t seem to fear death because he seemed to own it.
"So you’re the one who’s been hiding beneath our city all this time," Apollo said finally.
His voice broke the tension not with a shout, but with the controlled power of a man who commanded the very essence of life.

His life affinity lent his words a resonant, harmonic quality that carried effortlessly through the narrow passage, vibrating against the stone walls until even the soldiers at the very rear of both formations could hear his challenge.
"Lord Xerollion...
We finally meet face to face."
"Apollo Brightsoul."
The response came from behind the mask, but it wasn’t the voice of the man they knew as Rex.
This voice was lower, a gravelly register that seemed to vibrate from the floorboards of the world itself.
It was deliberately weighted, pitched to carry menace rather than any semblance of human warmth.
"Your reputation reached me long before you did..."
"The songs of your bravery precede you."
"They tell me you lead this force with great courage, which I suppose is one way of describing how far you’ve marched into territory that was never yours."
Apollo’s eyes flashed with holy fire.
"This territory sits beneath a city that has buried more of its own over the past several months than it did in the previous twenty years combined."
"We’ve seen the bodies, Xerollion...
We’ve seen the aftermath."
"Cities bury people, Brightsoul," Xerollion replied, his tone conversational, almost bored.
"It’s one of the few things they are actually designed for."
A sharp intake of breath hissed through the Aethelgard ranks.
Valentina stepped forward half a pace, her boots clicking like a death knell against the stone.
Unlike Apollo’s measured diplomacy, her voice was a blade cold, accusatory, and honed by months of grief.
"Let’s not pretend this is some philosophical debate about urban planning," Valentina snapped, her eyes blazing with the fury of a woman who had watched her students die in terror.
"There is a figure who calls himself The Undead Bringer, who has butchered apostles in their own beds, in places where our wards should have made them untouchable.
"There is an entity called Tremor who leveled our northern district, turning stone to powder and civilians to meat in a single afternoon."
"There is a half-dragon operative who nearly burned Aethelgard to its foundations."
"Every thread of every investigation, every drop of blood we’ve scraped off our streets, leads down here."
"Into your territory...
Into structures you control."
She took another step, her hand hovering near the hilt of her weapon.
"So I am going to ask you directly, in front of both our armies..."
"How much of that was the Underlayer’s doing?"
The question hung in the air like a guillotine blade suspended by a thread.
For several agonizing seconds, the only sound was the distant dripping of water and the ragged breathing of thousands of terrified men.
During that pause, Xerollion’s head turned.
It was a miniscule movement, barely an inch, toward Mordecai Vrael standing behind him.
It was too subtle for the soldiers to read, but to Apollo, it felt like a silent accusation. ’Is he looking at his accomplice?
Or is he reminding him of his debt?’
"The Underlayer is not a single hand, Valentina," Xerollion said at last, his voice cutting through the tension like a scalpel.
"It is two hundred thousand souls living in a dimensional layer that your city has treated as a garbage pit for eight centuries."
"You dump your sins here and expect them not to fester."
He took a single step forward, and the Underlayer soldiers behind him shifted in unison, their armor clanking with the sound of approaching doom.
"Things move in the dark."
"Some of them move with my knowledge."
"Some of them move simply because the filth and corruption your people created made their movement inevitable."
"If you want me to stand here and confess to the specific authorship of every catastrophe that has ’inconvenienced’ Aethelgard, you’ll be disappointed."
His masked head tilted slightly, the dim crystal light catching the edge of his visor.
"But if you want me to deny that the Underlayer has been involved in your recent suffering, you’ll be lying to yourself."
"And I have absolutely no interest in helping you maintain your delusions."

chapters.title: Chapter 1137. I Call It Walking Into a Den Because You Thought the Door Was Open
paragraphs: Behind the cold obsidian of his mask, Rex allowed himself a flicker of dark amusement. ’Technically true, utterly infuriating, and perfectly ambiguous.’
It was a masterpiece of linguistic manipulation. He watched the immediate fallout: the way the Aethelgard soldiers’ grip tightened on their spears, the way their eyes darted with newfound suspicion.
He had given them exactly what they needed to fuel their righteous fury: a confirmation of guilt wrapped in a shroud of plausible deniability.
But then, the fragile equilibrium of the standoff shattered.
Mordecai Vrael chose that exact moment to break.
He stepped forward, stumbling half a pace past the protective flanks of Cassandra and Gorvasha.

His movement was clumsy, lacking the lethal grace of the others, and his voice when it finally came was pitched higher than Rex’s, cracking with a genuine, desperate distress that cut through the oppressive silence.
"That isn’t... that isn’t a fair characterization!" Mordecai cried out, his hands lifting in a gesture of helpless protest. "I am the Demon Lord of this territory!"
"I never ordered an attack called Tremor!"
"I never sent the Undead Bringer to slaughter your people!" His chest heaved, his breathing shallow and audible even to the front ranks. "I heard those names the same way you did!"
"I read the reports with horror, just as you did!"
"Whatever those monsters were, whatever carnage they wrought... they did not come from my throne!"

The declaration landed like a grenade in the center of the corridor. An immediate, visible ripple of confusion surged through both armies. On the Aethelgard side, the rigid formation wavered as soldiers exchanged uncertain glances.

Apollo Brightsoul didn’t move, but his entire posture shifted; his brow drew together in a hard furrow, one eyebrow lifting as his mind raced to process the contradiction. The Demon Lord was denying everything, while the man supposedly ruling him was frantically claiming innocence.
’Is this a civil war?’ Apollo wondered, his inner voice sharp with calculation. ’Or is he lying? Is this a performance to sow doubt?’
Behind his mask, Rex savored the exquisite irony. He watched Mordecai deliver, with complete and terrifying sincerity, the single most valuable piece of misdirection he had ever orchestrated.
The idiot genuinely believed he was defending his honor. He had no conception that his bewildered honesty was the final brushstroke needed to complete the lie.
By appearing out of the loop, Mordecai made the Underlayer look exactly as Rex intended: a fractured, chaotic ecosystem where independent monsters could emerge without central command.
A frightened, confused scapegoat who believed in his own innocence was worth more than ten thousand trained liars.
Valentina, however, was not so easily swayed by the theatrics of a panicked demon. Her instincts, honed by years of hunting shadows, screamed that something was wrong.
She caught the discrepancy immediately—the gap between Xerollion’s cold evasion and Mordecai’s frantic denial—and she latched onto it like a predator.
Her gaze shifted away from Apollo, her eyes narrowing into slits of icy accusation as she fixed them on Rex. The air around her seemed to drop several degrees as her magical aura began to prickle.
"Interesting," she said, her voice dropping to a dangerous, razor-edged whisper that carried a lethal weight. "Your Demon Lord denies the very atrocities you refuse to disavow."
She took a step forward, her hand closing around the hilt of her blade with enough force to whiten her knuckles. "So let’s cut through the theater, Lord Xerollion."
"Which is it? Do you hold absolute authority over every drop of blood spilled in this realm, or is there something else moving in these tunnels—something so monstrous that even you cannot leash it?"
The masked head tilted just a fraction, a slow, deliberate motion that felt more like the assessment of a specimen than the reply of a man.
When the answer finally came, it carried the faintest, most dangerous edge of amusement—the sound of someone who had already won a game their opponent hadn’t even realized they were playing.
"True authority is never singular, Headmaster," Xerollion said, the title tasting like poison on his tongue. "Anyone who has truly wielded power knows that."
"A crown does not control every shadow it casts."

He took a single step forward, the obsidian plating of his armor catching the sickly blue light, making him look like a vengeful god carved from the abyss itself. "There are powers moving in this realm with purposes of their own."
"Some align with my interests; some are indifferent; and some would gladly see me buried alongside every last one of your soldiers if they believed the opportunity presented itself."
"But you are missing the point.
His voice dropped lower, becoming something intimate and terrifying. "What matters for you, Valentina, is not identifying which hand held which knife."

"What matters is that you have marched several thousand armed souls through a dimensional gate into a corridor where no amount of moral certainty or bureaucratic investigation will protect a single one of them."
"You have gone too far to turn this into an inquiry..."
"You have crossed the threshold."
"But now, you simply have to survive it."

The threat hung in the air like the smell of ozone before a lightning strike. The tension between the two armies was so visceral it felt as though the stone walls themselves might crack under the pressure.

Cassandra chose that moment to shatter the standoff. Her voice cut across the corridor with the sharp, contemptuous clarity that had once commanded entire divisions and sent lesser men fleeing in terror.
"It’s remarkable, honestly," she spat, her eyes burning with centuries of accumulated resentment. "Eight hundred years of Aethelgard treating this place as beneath their notice."
"Eight hundred years of dumping their exiles, their criminals, and their inconvenient problems down these shafts without so much as a second thought."
"And now that the consequences have finally crawled up to your doorstep, you arrive with your polished banners and your sanctimonious speeches about justice."

She took a step forward, her weapon humming with restrained energy. "Where was your justice when the first Underlayer settlements starved because your city sealed the trade shafts to ’purify’ the district?"
"Where was your justice when you cut off our oxygen to suffocate rebellion before it could even breathe?"

"Where was your justice," Gorvasha added, her voice a low, guttural growl that seemed to vibrate up from the very bedrock of the corridor, "when you sent your pathetic hunting parties down here to slaughter demons for sport and called it ’Apostle training’?"

The massive demoness loomed like a mountain of muscle and scarred flesh, her presence alone enough to make the front ranks of Aethelgard visibly recoil. "You march into a corridor you do not understand, in a realm whose geography you have never mapped, and you have the audacity to call it courage."
"I call it walking into a den because you thought the door was left open."
The silence that followed was different than before. It wasn’t the silence of fear; it was the silence of a fuse burning down to the powder keg.

The Aethelgard soldiers began to shift their weight, shields rising, spear tips lowering. The Underlayer warriors behind Xerollion didn’t move, but their energy shifted, a coiled spring of violence waiting for the first drop of blood to hit the floor.

chapters.title: Chapter 1138. A Plan That Was Completed Before Your Key Was Forged
paragraphs: The verbal assault escalated with the speed of a spreading wildfire. Accusations became projectiles, hurled across the narrow gap between the two armies with venomous intent.
Voices rose in a cacophony of rage: soldiers from Aethelgard shouted about duty and law, while the Underlayer warriors roared back with curses that spoke of centuries of accumulated hatred.

The temperature of the confrontation didn’t just rise; it became molten. On both flanks, the scrape of leather against armor and the creak of tightened sword hilts echoed through the stone passage as men prepared to die.

Apollo Brightsoul watched it all, his golden eyes tracking the movement of every tense muscle and every trembling finger. He let the chaos reign for exactly thirty seconds long enough to gauge the breaking point of both sides.
Then, he acted.
"ENOUGH."

The word wasn’t merely spoken; it was commanded. He channeled the raw resonance of his life affinity into his voice, sending a harmonic shockwave through the corridor that physically seemed to push against the noise.
The effect was instantaneous. The shouting died mid-breath, and the only sound left was the ragged, angry breathing of thousands.

"I did not march four thousand people down here to debate the grievances of dead centuries," Apollo said, his voice steady despite the inferno of emotion swirling around him. "Whatever hatred this realm holds against Aethelgard, and I am not naive enough to think every accusation is fabricated; none of it justifies the atrocities committed against my people."
His face hardened into something resembling granite. "Children in our outer districts were aged backward by magic no scholar could identify, their bodies withered into nothingness before their eyes."
"Families have been forced to bury empty coffins because there was nothing left of their loved ones but ash and memory."
"That ends today... one way or another."
He stepped forward, the light from his own aura casting long, imposing shadows behind him. He fixed his gaze directly on the obsidian visor of Rex’s mask.
"Surrender yourself peacefully, Lord Xerollion."
"Come with us... Answer for these crimes in a court of law, and I will use every ounce of my authority to ensure this ends without another drop of blood being spilled in this tunnel."
"That is my only offer... Take it, and we walk away."
For a heartbeat, there was absolute stillness. Then came the laugh.
It wasn’t a roar. It wasn’t a theatrical cackle.
It was a quiet, dry sound—the sound of someone who had just heard something so profoundly delusional that it bordered on comedy. That quietness made it infinitely worse than any shout.
It carried the genuine amusement of a man who had been offered a pittance when he already owned the mountain.

"You have built something remarkable in your mind, Apostle," Xerollion said, his voice dripping with condescension. "A fantasy where I simply hand you the keys to my kingdom because you asked politely and wrapped your demands in the language of mercy."
Rex took a slow step forward, the movement precise and predatory. "I want you to understand something before the slaughter begins properly, Brightsoul.
"You do not yet comprehend the scale of what you are standing in front of."
"You think you are negotiating with a warlord who can be reasoned down from a position of strength..."
"You think this is a standoff."
His masked head tilted, and for the first time, there was something truly monstrous beneath the words. "You are not negotiating with a man."
"You are negotiating with the inevitable outcome of a plan that was completed before your key was even forged."
"You haven’t walked into a trap... You have walked into an execution."
The tension in the corridor passed the point of no return. It became a physical, crushing weight that made lungs feel tight and hearts hammer against ribs.
Every hand along both front lines was white-knuckled around steel. The air tasted of blood before a single wound had been dealt.

In the Aethelgard formation, a young soldier, his face pale with terror, suffered a momentary lapse in nerve. His sweaty grip slipped on his spear haft, and the weapon clattered against the stone floor with a sharp, echoing crack.
In that moment of silence, the sound was as deafening as a thunderclap. It was the starter’s signal.
Valentina didn’t hesitate. She didn’t wait for an order from Apollo.
Her hand shot up, her fingers splayed in a command that transcended words. Her eyes were fixed on Xerollion with a hunter’s singular focus.
"Negotiation is finished," she commanded, her voice carrying with lethal clarity to the furthest ranks of her army. "All divisions ENGAGE!"
Apollo gave a single, grim nod, the silent acknowledgment between commanders before the slaughter began. He retreated half a step, sliding into a low combat stance that radiated authority.
The golden glow along his forearms and shoulders didn’t just brighten; it intensified, pulsing like the heartbeat of a sun, as his Life affinity spiraled upward in preparation for the cataclysm.
Across the narrow gap, Rex didn’t move with urgency. He raised a single hand slowly, palm open, in a gesture of casual dismissal.
The effect was terrifying. As if connected by some invisible nerve, the entire Underlayer formation shifted in perfect unison.
Thousands of soldiers dropped into deadly, practiced stances in a single coordinated motion that rippled backward through the corridor like a tsunami moving through deep water.
For one more heartbeat, there was a vacuum of sound, a terrible, expectant silence where the world seemed to hold its breath.
Then, reality shattered.

The first collision wasn’t just a sound; it was an assault on the senses. It was the wet crunch of steel meeting bone, the thunderous detonation of magical barriers, and a collective shriek of thousands that reverberated off the stone walls, amplifying until it felt like the corridor itself was screaming.

The gap between the two armies didn’t close; it evaporated. In less than three seconds, the two masses of humanity and monstrosity slammed together with such force that the shockwave knocked nearby soldiers off their feet.
The engagement immediately devolved into a claustrophobic hellscape. In the crush, there was no room for elegant swordplay or tactical maneuvering.

It became a meat grinder. Bodies were pressed so tightly together that men could taste the copper tang of each other’s blood. Weapons became useless in the press, forcing soldiers to rely on daggers, teeth, and broken gauntlets.
Elemental flashes of sickly greens, searing whites, and arterial reds strobed through the passage, casting grotesque, flickering shadows that burned into the retinas of everyone present.
Apollo drove into the Underlayer’s front rank like a living projectile. His entire body was wreathed in a corona of golden light, but it was no longer the gentle radiance of healing.
It was a corrupted, pressurized force. Where his aura touched the enemy, the effect was nightmarish: demons would stagger as if decades of age had been forced into their marrow in a single heartbeat.
Their joints seized with audible cracks, their flesh withered, and their vitality was forcibly drained away in a twisted reversal of his affinity’s purpose.
One demon, lunging with a rusted blade, suddenly shriveled into a husk of desiccated skin and bone before Apollo’s fist connected with its skull, shattering the weakened bone like dry porcelain.
’Focus,’ Apollo commanded himself, his inner voice a cold anchor in the storm of violence. ’Four minutes.’
’I have four minutes of full activation before the backlash tears me apart.’
’Don’t waste a second on the weak.’
At his right shoulder, Elliot Von Starlight moved like a streak of lightning. The white blaze of his Heroic Strike pulsed in perfect synchronization with Apollo’s rhythm.
Their coordination was terrifyingly efficient. Apollo would soften a section of the demonic line, his golden pressure slowing their reflexes to a crawl, and then Elliot would strike.

The Heroic Strike landed in the weakened gaps with concussive force so devastating it didn’t just kill; it obliterated. A demon sergeant was caught mid-swing, his chest cavity collapsing inward with a wet, sucking sound as he was hurled backward into his own comrades, his ribs splintering through his armor.
"That’s three lines!" Elliot shouted, his voice raw as he ducked under a clawed swing and drove his blade through a throat.
He flashed a grin at Apollo, though it was stained with fresh blood spattered across his cheek. "Three lines in under two minutes!"
"We’re tearing through them faster than the projections said we would!"
"Don’t get fucking greedy, Elliot!" Apollo roared back, his voice cracking like thunder.

He pivoted on his heel, catching an enraged axeman mid-lunge. Instead of a blade, Apollo met the demon’s chest with an open palm charged with concentrated life force. The impact sounded like a sledgehammer hitting wet clay.
The demon’s sternum imploded, spraying crimson across the stones as he crumpled into a broken heap. "Faster than projected means we’re deeper into their territory than planned."
"The further we push, the more dangerous the meat grinder becomes!"
"Watch your flanks or you’ll die screaming!"
