The air tasted of blood before a single wound had been dealt.
In the Aethelgard formation, a young soldier, his face pale with terror, suffered a momentary lapse in nerve.
His sweaty grip slipped on his spear haft, and the weapon clattered against the stone floor with a sharp, echoing crack.
In that moment of silence, the sound was as deafening as a thunderclap.
It was the starter’s signal.
Valentina didn’t hesitate.
She didn’t wait for an order from Apollo.
Her hand shot up, her fingers splayed in a command that transcended words.
Her eyes were fixed on Xerollion with a hunter’s singular focus.
"Negotiation is finished," she commanded, her voice carrying with lethal clarity to the furthest ranks of her army.
"All divisions ENGAGE!"
Apollo gave a single, grim nod, the silent acknowledgment between commanders before the slaughter began.
He retreated half a step, sliding into a low combat stance that radiated authority.
The golden glow along his forearms and shoulders didn’t just brighten; it intensified, pulsing like the heartbeat of a sun, as his Life affinity spiraled upward in preparation for the cataclysm.
Across the narrow gap, Rex didn’t move with urgency.
He raised a single hand slowly, palm open, in a gesture of casual dismissal.
The effect was terrifying.
As if connected by some invisible nerve, the entire Underlayer formation shifted in perfect unison.
Thousands of soldiers dropped into deadly, practiced stances in a single coordinated motion that rippled backward through the corridor like a tsunami moving through deep water.
For one more heartbeat, there was a vacuum of sound, a terrible, expectant silence where the world seemed to hold its breath.
Then, reality shattered.
The first collision wasn’t just a sound; it was an assault on the senses.

It was the wet crunch of steel meeting bone, the thunderous detonation of magical barriers, and a collective shriek of thousands that reverberated off the stone walls, amplifying until it felt like the corridor itself was screaming.
The gap between the two armies didn’t close; it evaporated.
In less than three seconds, the two masses of humanity and monstrosity slammed together with such force that the shockwave knocked nearby soldiers off their feet.
The engagement immediately devolved into a claustrophobic hellscape.
In the crush, there was no room for elegant swordplay or tactical maneuvering.
It became a meat grinder.
Bodies were pressed so tightly together that men could taste the copper tang of each other’s blood.
Weapons became useless in the press, forcing soldiers to rely on daggers, teeth, and broken gauntlets.
Elemental flashes of sickly greens, searing whites, and arterial reds strobed through the passage, casting grotesque, flickering shadows that burned into the retinas of everyone present.
Apollo drove into the Underlayer’s front rank like a living projectile.
His entire body was wreathed in a corona of golden light, but it was no longer the gentle radiance of healing.
It was a corrupted, pressurized force.
Where his aura touched the enemy, the effect was nightmarish: demons would stagger as if decades of age had been forced into their marrow in a single heartbeat.
Their joints seized with audible cracks, their flesh withered, and their vitality was forcibly drained away in a twisted reversal of his affinity’s purpose.
One demon, lunging with a rusted blade, suddenly shriveled into a husk of desiccated skin and bone before Apollo’s fist connected with its skull, shattering the weakened bone like dry porcelain.
’Focus,’ Apollo commanded himself, his inner voice a cold anchor in the storm of violence. ’Four minutes.’
’I have four minutes of full activation before the backlash tears me apart.’
’Don’t waste a second on the weak.’
At his right shoulder, Elliot Von Starlight moved like a streak of lightning.
The white blaze of his Heroic Strike pulsed in perfect synchronization with Apollo’s rhythm.
Their coordination was terrifyingly efficient.
Apollo would soften a section of the demonic line, his golden pressure slowing their reflexes to a crawl, and then Elliot would strike.
The Heroic Strike landed in the weakened gaps with concussive force so devastating it didn’t just kill; it obliterated.
A demon sergeant was caught mid-swing, his chest cavity collapsing inward with a wet, sucking sound as he was hurled backward into his own comrades, his ribs splintering through his armor.
"That’s three lines!" Elliot shouted, his voice raw as he ducked under a clawed swing and drove his blade through a throat.
He flashed a grin at Apollo, though it was stained with fresh blood spattered across his cheek.
"Three lines in under two minutes!"
"We’re tearing through them faster than the projections said we would!"
"Don’t get fucking greedy, Elliot!" Apollo roared back, his voice cracking like thunder.
He pivoted on his heel, catching an enraged axeman mid-lunge.
Instead of a blade, Apollo met the demon’s chest with an open palm charged with concentrated life force.
The impact sounded like a sledgehammer hitting wet clay.
The demon’s sternum imploded, spraying crimson across the stones as he crumpled into a broken heap.
"Faster than projected means we’re deeper into their territory than planned."
"The further we push, the more dangerous the meat grinder becomes!"
"Watch your flanks or you’ll die screaming!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1139. That Voice Resonated With a Memory She Couldn’t Grasp
paragraphs: Elliot let out a laugh, not a manic one, but something raw and almost desperate, filled with the intoxicating relief of a man who had finally found his purpose.

For months, he had carried the gnawing guilt of a coward who had chased personal mastery while his city bled; now, standing in the center of a screaming hellscape with Apollo at his back, that guilt was incinerated.
"This is it!" he roared, his voice cracking with adrenaline. "This is what we trained for!"

His blade erupted in a blinding corona of Heroic Strike energy as he plunged forward, the fourth defensive line buckling like rotted wood under the combined pressure of his fury and Apollo’s relentless advance.
While the center of the corridor became a churning vortex of golden light and demonic screams, Evelyn Astralight moved through the chaos like a ghost woven from starlight.

For two years, Evelyn had played a dangerous game of deception. She had moved through the world with deliberate restraint, revealing barely forty percent of her true capabilities, a habit born from the cold, calculating instinct of a reincarnator who knew that to reveal one’s full hand was to invite certain death.
But today, the pretense shattered. Today, she stopped pretending to be mortal.

She moved with a speed that defied physics, crossing thirty meters of packed, blood-slicked corridor in less than a heartbeat. To the soldiers around her, she was nothing more than a blur of silver and white.
To the demons in her path, she was an inevitable catastrophe. She didn’t swing wildly; she struck with the surgical precision of a god.
Her blade found the soft gaps between armor plates, severing tendons at the kneecaps, punching through nerve clusters in necks, and splitting skulls with terrifying accuracy.

Behind her, a chain reaction of collapses followed like the wake of a predator: twelve demons crumpled simultaneously, their legs severed or their spines shattered before their brains could even register an attack.
Twenty more followed in rapid succession, their bodies dropping in a grotesque domino effect as their commanders screamed futile orders that died in their throats.

’Faster, sharper, don’t breathe, don’t think,’ Evelyn commanded herself, her inner monologue a cold stream of tactical calculations amidst the sensory overload. ’The blood is slick. Watch the footing. Three demons on the left flank approaching strike, move, repeat.’
Yet, despite the lethal rhythm of her dance, something kept pulling at her attention.
Something wrong.
Something that made the hair on her arms stand up even as she carved through flesh.
Her eyes kept darting toward the dead center of the Underlayer formation.
The masked figure Xerollion had not moved.
In the midst of a massacre where every inch of ground was bought with screams and arterial spray, he remained an impossible island of stillness.

He stood at the heart of the demonic storm, unmoved by the vibrations of earth-shaking magic or the wet thud of corpses hitting the stone. He wasn’t commanding; he wasn’t shouting orders to rally his troops.
He was simply... present.
’Why isn’t he engaging?’ Evelyn wondered, the thought slicing through her focus. ’Is he arrogant? Or is he waiting?’
It wasn’t the stillness of a general watching his chess pieces move. It was something far more sinister than the stillness of an architect watching a clockwork mechanism unfold exactly as designed.
He wasn’t watching a battle; he was watching a process. He was watching an inevitability.
And beneath that tactical unease lay something more personal, something that gnawed at the back of her mind like a splinter she couldn’t reach.

There was a cadence to his presence, a specific, unhurried weight to the way he held himself that felt achingly familiar. Every time she caught a glimpse of that obsidian armor through the strobing magical lights, her heart gave a traitorous flutter of recognition.
That voice, the way it had cut through the paralysis, resonated with a memory she couldn’t quite grasp, a ghost of a feeling she had been trying to pin down since the moment he first spoke.
’Not now,’ she snarled internally, forcing the recognition down into the darkest corner of her mind. ’You can’t afford to hesitate.’
’If you lose focus now, you’re just another corpse in this tunnel.’
With a snarl of frustration, she pivoted, her blade singing as it severed the arm of an approaching demon, burying her focus back into the brutal necessity of survival.
There would be time to solve the mystery of the mask later, assuming there was any ’later’ left for her to see.

Valentina did not fight like a soldier; she fought like an architect rearranging the fundamental laws of physics. While the center of the corridor was a chaotic meat grinder of steel and sinew, she held the rear third with a terrifying, methodical dominance that reminded every living soul present why she had occupied the highest seat at the Grand Academy for decades.

Her magic was not explosive; it was structural. With precise, sweeping gestures of her hands, she wove interlocking barrier matrices across the span of the corridor—translucent geometric webs that didn’t just block incoming spellfire but consumed it.

When a demon sorcerer unleashed a torrent of sickly green necrotic energy, Valentina didn’t flinch. Her barrier caught the spell and absorbed its momentum with a resonant hummm, and then she redirected the overflow.
With a sharp flick of her wrist, she vented the redirected energy into the stone floor, causing the ground beneath a flanking demon squad to detonate in a spray of shrapnel and pulverized rock.
’Layer one: containment.’
’Layer two: redirection.’
’Layer three: annihilation,’ she cataloged silently, her mind a flawless machine.
Her breathing remained eerily steady, a slow, controlled rhythm that stood in stark contrast to the ragged gasps of the dying around her.
Her soldiers watched her back like she was a lighthouse in a hurricane; as long as Valentina remained calm, the slaughter felt like something that could be won.

Behind her, Morwenna Nightwing commanded the reserves with the lethal economy of a woman who had spent thirty years teaching others how to die properly. There was no wasted motion in her combat stance.

Every parry she executed was not merely defensive; it was a setup. When a demon blade whistled toward her throat, she didn’t just deflect it; she caught the momentum on her vambrace, twisted her hips, and drove her elbow into the creature’s windpipe with a wet crunch that echoed off the ceiling.
"Close the gap on the left!"
"Third rank, pivot three degrees... NOW!" Morwenna barked, her voice cutting through the cacophony without ever breaking into panic. "Don’t let them exploit the stagger!"
"Hold the line or lose your heads!
Her Nightwing elites moved like extensions of her own body. They didn’t need complex orders; they read the shift in her shoulders and the tilt of her blade and adjusted their formation instinctively.

She moved through the blood-slicked passage like a reaper, pulling soldiers back from collapsing positions just seconds before they would have been overwhelmed, her blade a silver streak that left severed limbs and arterial sprays in its wake.
Yet, beneath the iron discipline of her combat stance, Morwenna’s mind was betraying her.
In the brief, microscopic pauses between strikes, the split second after a demon’s skull split under her boot, her thoughts fled from the gore to something she had buried deeper than any wound.
A memory.

A sun-drenched morning in her own household, the smell of lavender and expensive tea, and a secret she had never whispered to another living soul. The memory burned brighter than the magical fires consuming the tunnel.
’Focus, damn you,’ she hissed at herself, her inner voice dripping with self-loathing as she parried a spiked mace. ’The Nightwing name isn’t built on secrets.’
’It’s built on blood and steel.’
She knew the stakes. This wasn’t just about survival; it was about legacy.

Every killing blow she landed, every flawless maneuver she executed, was a testament carved in flesh. If she faltered here, if she showed even a crack in her legendary composure, the Nightwing household would be reduced to footnotes in history.
She wasn’t just fighting for Aethelgard; she was fighting to ensure that when the survivors spoke of this day, they spoke of the Nightwing contribution with awe, not pity.
The tension in the air began to shift. The clash of steel was being overtaken by something more primal: the grinding of magical energies.

The air grew heavy and ionized, tasting of copper and burnt ozone. The magical pressure was building to a breaking point, the very stones of the corridor beginning to vibrate as the true power of the two armies prepared to collide in a final, devastating magical crescendo.
Twenty meters above the carnage, perched on a jagged shelf of granite that jutted from the eastern wall like a broken fang, Talyra Skydancer became an extension of her bowstring.
She was no longer a woman; she was a machine of lethal geometry.
Thwip crack!
Her first arrow punched through the eye socket of a demon berserker just as it raised a spiked mace over a fallen Aethelgard sergeant.
Before the corpse had even hit the blood-slicked stone, Talyra had already drawn again. Her fingers moved with a hypnotic, terrifying economy of motion: nock, draw, anchor, release.
Each arrow found the impossible gaps: the seam beneath an armpit, the slit in a visor, and the soft flesh behind a knee. Each shot was punctuated by the wet thunk of steel meeting meat.
’Two targets down... Three more closing on the left flank...’
’Shift angle...’

chapters.title: Chapter 1140. A Bowl-Shaped Depression, a Kill Box Reinforced for Three Weeks
paragraphs: Her eyes swept the battlefield, not with the panicked desperation of the dying, but with the cold assessment of a predator. But beneath that deadly focus, a poison was spreading through her mind.
She knew she knew that this massacre wasn’t a surprise. She knew the gears of this war had been turning long before the first blade was drawn.
Rex had orchestrated this. The realization didn’t make her tremble; it made her aim unnaturally steady, but it left a bitter, metallic taste in her mouth that no amount of adrenaline could wash away.
’We’re all just pieces on his board,’ she thought, her jaw tightening as she loosed another shaft that split a demon’s skull with a satisfying crunch. ’God helps us if he decides to flip the table.’
Below, in the shadow of the main engagement, Aisella Moonbloom was drowning in green light and crimson blood.
She worked the wounded line, a pale specter moving through a sea of agony. Her hands trailed soft, luminescent emerald energy, stitching together torn intestines and sealing gaping arterial sprays.
But the casualties were coming faster than the heartbeat of a dying man.
"Hold on! Stay with me!"
"Look at the light, don’t look at the wound!" Aisella screamed over the cacophony, her voice cracking.

She pressed her palms against the shattered ribcage of a young soldier, her magic burning hot as she forced bone to knit back together. The sound of grinding calcium filled her ears as she stabilized him, but the effort drained her like blood from an open vein.
Sweat glued strands of pale hair to her temples. Her hands began to betray her, developing a fine, uncontrollable tremor between patients.
’I can’t keep up.’
’There’s too much blood.’
’There’s too much death.’
But she couldn’t stop. She had given Rex her word she would be ready.

Every life she snatched back from the threshold of Hades was a shield she placed between him and the approaching darkness. Each successful healing felt like a temporary victory in a war that seemed determined to consume them all.
Meanwhile, Nerith Sylvarune had turned the corridor itself into a weapon.
She had found the damp, weeping seams where moisture seeped through the ancient stone, and she exploited them with vicious creativity.
"Rise and claim what is yours!" Nerith commanded, her voice echoing with primal authority.
She slammed her staff into the ground, and with a wet, tearing sound, schlorp thick, thorn-covered vines erupted from the stone cracks.

They coiled around demon ankles like emerald serpents, dragging entire squads off their feet with bone-snapping force. As demons fell, the vines tightened, crushing windpipes and splintering femurs with the relentless strength of growing timber.

For a fleeting second, between two devastating castings, a memory flickered through her mind: a sun-dappled Academy study room, the smell of old parchment, and the arrogant conviction she had voiced about nature always favoring the righteous.
A smile touched her lips, then vanished as quickly as it came, replaced by a hollow ache she couldn’t explain.
’Nature doesn’t favor the righteous,’ she realized grimly as she watched a vine crush a demon’s skull like an overripe melon. ’Nature only favors what survives.’
On the left flank, Mireya Snowlith was a blizzard contained in human form.
She fought with a ferocity that bordered on suicidal, her sword wreathed in frost and her magic singing a high, deadly note. She didn’t just fight the demons; she froze them.
With a precise thrust, she would flash freeze a cluster of enemies into brittle statues of ice, then follow through with a devastating horizontal slash.
CRACK SHATTER!
The sound of ice exploding was as constant as the screams. Shards of frozen flesh and bone sprayed across the corridor like deadly shrapnel.
Her usual icy composure had shattered, replaced by something raw and desperate. She fought like a woman trying to outrun a ghost, her blade carving through demon flesh with a vengeful hunger.
She needed this, needed the violence to drown out the memory of that canyon months ago, the memory of the sin she carried, a sin committed not by her own hand, but one that still stained her soul.

’More blood. More ice. More noise,’ Mireya thought frantically as she ducked under a swing, her blade severing a demon’s arm in a spray of black ichor. ’Just let me fight until there’s nothing left to kill.’

Ten minutes into the slaughter, the very bones of the Underlayer began to betray Aethelgard’s grand design. The corridor was not a battlefield; it was a digestive system, and the soldiers were being slowly chewed to pulp.
The geography was treacherous, a shifting labyrinth of widening chambers that suddenly constricted into suffocating gaps barely eight meters across.
Every time the Aethelgard advance attempted to press through these narrow throats, the tactical superiority of their numbers transformed into a death sentence.
What should have been a disciplined phalanx became a panicked mass of crushing flesh.
Ranks compressed so tightly that soldiers in the third and fourth lines couldn’t even raise their shields without striking their own comrades.
Long spears, the pride of their formation, became useless splinters of wood, jammed at awkward angles against the weeping stone walls.
"Hold the line! Don’t push so close, you fools!"
"Give them room to breathe!" an officer screamed, but his voice was drowned out by the wet thwack of demon blades finding soft bellies.

But the Underlayer defenders were not fighting a war of attrition; they were fighting a war of physics. Drilled relentlessly under Cassandra’s doctrine, they operated with the mechanical precision of a slaughterhouse.
They rotated through the choke points in ninety-second shifts, fresh, adrenaline-fueled killers replacing blood-soaked, exhausted men.

The Aethelgard front rank had no such mercy; they fought until their muscles seized, then fought until they died, their bodies becoming part of the obstacle that tripped their own retreating comrades.
Apollo, watching from a tactical vantage point, felt the sweat prickle his neck. His tactical mind screamed warnings that his pride refused to acknowledge.
’The formation is collapsing.’
’We’re feeding them corpses to slow us down.’ Realizing the slaughter at the second choke point was unsustainable, he made the desperate call. "Pull back the advance!"
"Redirect along the southern seam!"
"The fault line uses the broader shelf!
It was a gamble that seemed to pay off. Elliot, his face twisted in a mask of divine fury, unleashed his Heroic Strike.
The air shrieked as a lance of pure energy tore through the defensive wall along the southern seam. The stone exploded in a shower of sparks and debris.
"NOW! THROUGH THE BREACH!" Elliot roared.
Three hundred Aethelgard soldiers charged through the hole, their battle cries echoing like thunder for a hundred meters down the tunnel.
But they weren’t charging into victory. They were charging into a trap designed with sadistic perfection.
The breach hadn’t been a failure of defense; it had been a gift from Gorvasha.

The moment the Aethelgard surge committed to the southern shelf, the Orcish defenders began their performance. They retreated with theatrical panic, their screams convincing the humans that the line had truly shattered.

The soldiers poured into the space, their boots pounding on the floor, unaware that they were flowing directly into a bowl-shaped depression, a kill box Gorvasha had spent three weeks reinforcing with structural enchantments and hidden supports.
Gorvasha stood at the northern rim, her eyes burning with a cold, calculating hunger.
"Now," she growled, the word barely audible over the thunder of boots. "Die in the dark."
She swung her massive warhammer in a devastating arc, bringing it down on a pre-weakened seam of rock at the depression’s edge with a sound like a mountain cracking open. KRA THOOM!
The ceiling didn’t just fall; it surrendered. A ten-ton slab of ancient granite tore free from the overhead supports and plunged downward.
The sound was a deafening, grinding, screaming avalanche of stone that sealed the entrance behind the breaching force with the finality of a tombstone.
Two hundred Aethelgard soldiers were instantly pulverized beneath the impact, their screams cut short by the wet crunch of collapsing ribcages and skulls.
The remaining soldiers were trapped in a stone coffin with no exit, while four hundred Underlayer defenders perched on the high rim above them like vultures.
"Kill them all!" the command rang out from above. "Leave nothing but bone!"

For eleven minutes, the bowl became a charnel house. The sounds echoing from the depression were primal: the rhythmic thud of hammers, the wet tearing of flesh, and the inhuman shrieks of men realizing they were already dead.

The defenders rained down magical fire and crossbow bolts from the heights, while those inside the bowl fought with the desperation of cornered rats, their blades finding only blood and stone. Bone splintered under boots; entrails slicked the floor, making every footing a deadly gamble.
When Valentina finally intervened, her magic tore through the collapsed barrier from the outside with a brilliant, searing explosion of force; the aftermath was horrific.

As the dust settled and the new opening was revealed, only sixty-one Aethelgard soldiers stumbled out. They weren’t soldiers anymore; they were hollow-eyed wraiths, their armor shattered, their minds broken by eleven minutes of contained, concentrated slaughter.
They wandered past the main engagement like ghosts, incapable of holding a sword, their spirits left behind in the crimson-soaked bowl of the Underlayer.

sentences.text: Her eyes swept the battlefield, not with the panicked desperation of the dying, but with the cold assessment of a predator.
But beneath that deadly focus, a poison was spreading through her mind.
She knew she knew that this massacre wasn’t a surprise.
She knew the gears of this war had been turning long before the first blade was drawn.
Rex had orchestrated this.
The realization didn’t make her tremble; it made her aim unnaturally steady, but it left a bitter, metallic taste in her mouth that no amount of adrenaline could wash away.
’We’re all just pieces on his board,’ she thought, her jaw tightening as she loosed another shaft that split a demon’s skull with a satisfying crunch. ’God helps us if he decides to flip the table.’
Below, in the shadow of the main engagement, Aisella Moonbloom was drowning in green light and crimson blood.
She worked the wounded line, a pale specter moving through a sea of agony.
Her hands trailed soft, luminescent emerald energy, stitching together torn intestines and sealing gaping arterial sprays.
But the casualties were coming faster than the heartbeat of a dying man.
"Hold on!
Stay with me!"
"Look at the light, don’t look at the wound!" Aisella screamed over the cacophony, her voice cracking.
She pressed her palms against the shattered ribcage of a young soldier, her magic burning hot as she forced bone to knit back together.
The sound of grinding calcium filled her ears as she stabilized him, but the effort drained her like blood from an open vein.
Sweat glued strands of pale hair to her temples.
Her hands began to betray her, developing a fine, uncontrollable tremor between patients.
’I can’t keep up.’
’There’s too much blood.’
’There’s too much death.’
But she couldn’t stop.
She had given Rex her word she would be ready.
Every life she snatched back from the threshold of Hades was a shield she placed between him and the approaching darkness.
Each successful healing felt like a temporary victory in a war that seemed determined to consume them all.
Meanwhile, Nerith Sylvarune had turned the corridor itself into a weapon.
She had found the damp, weeping seams where moisture seeped through the ancient stone, and she exploited them with vicious creativity.
"Rise and claim what is yours!" Nerith commanded, her voice echoing with primal authority.
She slammed her staff into the ground, and with a wet, tearing sound, schlorp thick, thorn-covered vines erupted from the stone cracks.
They coiled around demon ankles like emerald serpents, dragging entire squads off their feet with bone-snapping force.
As demons fell, the vines tightened, crushing windpipes and splintering femurs with the relentless strength of growing timber.

For a fleeting second, between two devastating castings, a memory flickered through her mind: a sun-dappled Academy study room, the smell of old parchment, and the arrogant conviction she had voiced about nature always favoring the righteous.
A smile touched her lips, then vanished as quickly as it came, replaced by a hollow ache she couldn’t explain.
’Nature doesn’t favor the righteous,’ she realized grimly as she watched a vine crush a demon’s skull like an overripe melon. ’Nature only favors what survives.’
On the left flank, Mireya Snowlith was a blizzard contained in human form.
She fought with a ferocity that bordered on suicidal, her sword wreathed in frost and her magic singing a high, deadly note.
She didn’t just fight the demons; she froze them.
With a precise thrust, she would flash freeze a cluster of enemies into brittle statues of ice, then follow through with a devastating horizontal slash.
CRACK SHATTER!
The sound of ice exploding was as constant as the screams.
Shards of frozen flesh and bone sprayed across the corridor like deadly shrapnel.
Her usual icy composure had shattered, replaced by something raw and desperate.
She fought like a woman trying to outrun a ghost, her blade carving through demon flesh with a vengeful hunger.
She needed this, needed the violence to drown out the memory of that canyon months ago, the memory of the sin she carried, a sin committed not by her own hand, but one that still stained her soul.
’More blood.
More ice.
More noise,’ Mireya thought frantically as she ducked under a swing, her blade severing a demon’s arm in a spray of black ichor. ’Just let me fight until there’s nothing left to kill.’
Ten minutes into the slaughter, the very bones of the Underlayer began to betray Aethelgard’s grand design.
The corridor was not a battlefield; it was a digestive system, and the soldiers were being slowly chewed to pulp.
The geography was treacherous, a shifting labyrinth of widening chambers that suddenly constricted into suffocating gaps barely eight meters across.
Every time the Aethelgard advance attempted to press through these narrow throats, the tactical superiority of their numbers transformed into a death sentence.
What should have been a disciplined phalanx became a panicked mass of crushing flesh.
Ranks compressed so tightly that soldiers in the third and fourth lines couldn’t even raise their shields without striking their own comrades.
Long spears, the pride of their formation, became useless splinters of wood, jammed at awkward angles against the weeping stone walls.
"Hold the line!
Don’t push so close, you fools!"
"Give them room to breathe!" an officer screamed, but his voice was drowned out by the wet thwack of demon blades finding soft bellies.
But the Underlayer defenders were not fighting a war of attrition; they were fighting a war of physics.
Drilled relentlessly under Cassandra’s doctrine, they operated with the mechanical precision of a slaughterhouse.
They rotated through the choke points in ninety-second shifts, fresh, adrenaline-fueled killers replacing blood-soaked, exhausted men.

The Aethelgard front rank had no such mercy; they fought until their muscles seized, then fought until they died, their bodies becoming part of the obstacle that tripped their own retreating comrades.
Apollo, watching from a tactical vantage point, felt the sweat prickle his neck.
His tactical mind screamed warnings that his pride refused to acknowledge.
’The formation is collapsing.’
’We’re feeding them corpses to slow us down.’ Realizing the slaughter at the second choke point was unsustainable, he made the desperate call.
"Pull back the advance!"
"Redirect along the southern seam!"
"The fault line uses the broader shelf!
It was a gamble that seemed to pay off.
Elliot, his face twisted in a mask of divine fury, unleashed his Heroic Strike.
The air shrieked as a lance of pure energy tore through the defensive wall along the southern seam.
The stone exploded in a shower of sparks and debris.
"NOW!
THROUGH THE BREACH!" Elliot roared.
Three hundred Aethelgard soldiers charged through the hole, their battle cries echoing like thunder for a hundred meters down the tunnel.
But they weren’t charging into victory.
They were charging into a trap designed with sadistic perfection.
The breach hadn’t been a failure of defense; it had been a gift from Gorvasha.
The moment the Aethelgard surge committed to the southern shelf, the Orcish defenders began their performance.
They retreated with theatrical panic, their screams convincing the humans that the line had truly shattered.

The soldiers poured into the space, their boots pounding on the floor, unaware that they were flowing directly into a bowl-shaped depression, a kill box Gorvasha had spent three weeks reinforcing with structural enchantments and hidden supports.
Gorvasha stood at the northern rim, her eyes burning with a cold, calculating hunger.
"Now," she growled, the word barely audible over the thunder of boots.
"Die in the dark."
She swung her massive warhammer in a devastating arc, bringing it down on a pre-weakened seam of rock at the depression’s edge with a sound like a mountain cracking open.
KRA THOOM!
The ceiling didn’t just fall; it surrendered.
A ten-ton slab of ancient granite tore free from the overhead supports and plunged downward.
The sound was a deafening, grinding, screaming avalanche of stone that sealed the entrance behind the breaching force with the finality of a tombstone.
Two hundred Aethelgard soldiers were instantly pulverized beneath the impact, their screams cut short by the wet crunch of collapsing ribcages and skulls.
The remaining soldiers were trapped in a stone coffin with no exit, while four hundred Underlayer defenders perched on the high rim above them like vultures.
"Kill them all!" the command rang out from above.
"Leave nothing but bone!"
For eleven minutes, the bowl became a charnel house.
The sounds echoing from the depression were primal: the rhythmic thud of hammers, the wet tearing of flesh, and the inhuman shrieks of men realizing they were already dead.
The defenders rained down magical fire and crossbow bolts from the heights, while those inside the bowl fought with the desperation of cornered rats, their blades finding only blood and stone.
Bone splintered under boots; entrails slicked the floor, making every footing a deadly gamble.
When Valentina finally intervened, her magic tore through the collapsed barrier from the outside with a brilliant, searing explosion of force; the aftermath was horrific.
As the dust settled and the new opening was revealed, only sixty-one Aethelgard soldiers stumbled out.
They weren’t soldiers anymore; they were hollow-eyed wraiths, their armor shattered, their minds broken by eleven minutes of contained, concentrated slaughter.
They wandered past the main engagement like ghosts, incapable of holding a sword, their spirits left behind in the crimson-soaked bowl of the Underlayer.

chapters.title: Chapter 1141. Let Them Think They Have Won, the Stone Will Do the Rest
paragraphs: Apollo stood frozen at the tactical overlook, his knuckles white as he gripped the hilt of his sword. Forty meters away, the southern shelf’s brilliant flanking maneuver hadn’t just failed; it had been systematically dismantled.
He watched through the haze of dust and magical discharge as the last of his hopeful soldiers were cut down in that godforsaken stone bowl.
A cold, oily suspicion slithered up his spine, settling in his gut like lead.
This wasn’t a battle.
This was a harvest.
’Every move I make... every tactical shift... they’re already there waiting.’
’It’s like they’ve seen this dance a thousand times before.’
"They knew," Apollo whispered, the words lost to the wind until he forced them out. "Gods above, they knew."
"Knew what, Apollo? Speak up!" Elliot roared as he charged past, his divine radiance flickering like a dying candle.

Blood ran freely from a jagged gash above his eyebrow, streaming down his face in crimson rivulets that stained his golden armor. He swung his blade in a desperate arc, severing a demon’s head with a wet squelch, but his eyes remained fixed on the chaos.
"Why aren’t you commanding?! The line is buckling!"
Apollo turned to him, his face pale beneath the grime. "They knew we were coming through that Key, Elliot!"
"Every angle, every choke point, every contingency—it was all laid out for us!"
"This entire corridor wasn’t built to defend the Underlayer! It was built to receive us!"
The grin that had sustained Elliot through three hours of carnage faltered. For the first time since the first demon drew blood, the light in his eyes dimmed, replaced by a hollow, gnawing dread.
"That’s impossible... We had intelligence... we had months of planning—"
"Intelligence we provided?!" Apollo snapped, though his voice lacked conviction.
A blur of motion announced Evelyn’s arrival. She appeared at Apollo’s shoulder with supernatural speed, her breathing barely elevated despite having sprinted across half a battlefield.
Her armor was splattered with black ichor and arterial spray.
"The eastern side is compromised too," she said, her voice clipped and urgent. "Every time I attempt a pincer, they have a secondary formation waiting in the shadows."
"They aren’t reacting to our movements, Apollo... They’re executing a script."
She grabbed his pauldron, forcing him to meet her gaze. "I’ve been in six major engagements against fortified positions."
"None of them looked like this... This isn’t defense; this is a trap that has been sprung from the moment we stepped through the portal."
Apollo looked back at the slaughter.
"Then we push harder," he said, though the words felt brittle, like ice cracking underfoot. "We overwhelm their preparations!"
"We break their plan by sheer force of will!"
But even as he said it, his mind screamed at him that they were merely feeding more meat into the grinder.
Behind them, cutting through the center of the formation like a scalpel through silk, Rex Rexilion moved with terrifying, measured competence. He was the eye of the storm.
A demon lunged at him, claws extended to rake his throat; without breaking stride, Rex pivoted, his blade finding the demon’s sternum with a sickening crunch of vertebrae.
He didn’t waste movement. And he didn’t waste breath.
Thwack. Slice. Step.
"Fall back to the secondary line!" Rex commanded, his voice calm, almost conversational amidst the screaming and the grinding of steel.
He grabbed two wounded soldiers by their harnesses, hauling them clear of a collapsing stone archway just as it shattered into lethal debris.
"Captain, flank left now!" he barked at a Nightwing officer, saving the man’s life seconds before a demon’s mace would have turned his skull into paste.
He was exactly where a legendary hero should be. He was the anchor, the reliable ally, the symbol of hope. He moved with a practiced grace that made the impossible look routine.
’But why does he look so bored?’ Apollo thought bitterly, watching Rex’s back. ’He’s fighting a war for survival, and he’s moving like he’s practicing a routine in a training hall.’
’His blade finds the heart, his footwork is flawless, but there’s no fire.’
’No desperation. Just... execution.’

Rex Rexilion continued his perfect work, a flawless soldier in a doomed army, while around him, the screams of Aethelgard rose higher, each one a note in a symphony of slaughter that he seemed to have written himself.
On the opposite side of the corridor, where the air tasted of copper and burnt ozone, the Underlayer unleashed its true answer.

Cassandra Vexmoor had been a patient predator. For eight agonizing minutes, she had stood like a statue of marble amidst the carnage, watching Aethelgard’s formations ripple and break, letting her standard soldiers absorb the initial shockwave of the invasion.
She was reading them not their numbers, but their souls. She was cataloging their desperation, their tactical weaknesses, and the exact rhythm of their slaughter.
Then, she moved.
The sudden shift in her posture made the nearest defenders flinch instinctively. With a fluid, almost ritualistic motion, she drew her blade across her own forearm.
But the blood that welled from the wound did not drip. It defied gravity, suspended in the air like liquid rubies.
It spread outward in a dark, pulsating corona that seemed to drink the very light from the corridor.
"Let the debt be paid in crimson," she hissed, her voice distorting into something ancient and terrifying.
The transformation didn’t just change her appearance; it rewrote reality around her. The Blood Oath Demon Queen erupted from the shell of the woman.
Her claws elongated into obsidian talons, and her blade ignited with a malevolent crimson energy that left searing afterimages hanging in the air like ghostly scars.
She moved with a speed that shattered the laws of physics. She didn’t run; she blurred.
Her first pass through Aethelgard’s left flank was less of a charge and more of a harvesting.
Squelch. Crack. Tear.
Eleven soldiers were decapitated or disemboweled in a single heartbeat. By her second pass, nine more were reduced to screaming heaps of severed limbs and shattered armor.
"Bind her! For the Light, bind her now!" an Apostle-ranked mage screamed, his hands weaving intricate geometric patterns.
A lattice of golden energy erupted toward Cassandra, designed to freeze a god in place.
Cassandra didn’t even slow down.
"Pathetic," she spat.

The blood energy bleeding from her skin dissolved the binding spell on contact, eating through the magical structure like acid through parchment. Before the mage could even register his failure, she closed the distance.
With a vicious backhanded strike, she caught him mid-incantation.
CRACK.

The sound of his ribs folding over her forearm was sickeningly wet. She didn’t stop there; she hurled his broken body into three of his own soldiers, using the dying man as a fleshy projectile to shatter their formation.

Amidst the wet sounds of evisceration, Cassandra’s crimson eyes flickered toward the center of the corridor. Through the haze of blood and magical discharge, she saw him, the masked figure, standing motionless, an island of eerie calm in a sea of screaming death.

’Is this what it means to be truly dangerous?’ she wondered, a flash of something complicated pride mixed with something darker stirring behind her eyes. ’To stand in the center of a hurricane you created and not even blink?’
She remembered the day she had knelt to him. She, the Demon Queen who had once brought entire military structures to their knees, had submitted to a mortal’s authority.

There had been nights of bitter reflection, wondering if she had traded her sovereignty for a gilded cage, if her choice had been a surrender dressed up as strategy. But watching him now, watching him orchestrate this genocide from the center of a grinder he had built with flawless precision, she knew.
It hadn’t been weakness. It had been the single sharpest strategic decision of her entire existence.
"Die for nothing," she growled, turning back to the slaughter and cleaving through four more soldiers before the thought could even fully form.

Not far from her, Gorvasha Bloodtusk was conducting her own symphony of destruction. If Cassandra was a scalpel, Gorvasha was a sledgehammer. She fought with a primordial brutality that made even the most battle-hardened Aethelgard veterans freeze in terror.
Her warhammer didn’t just hit shields; it obliterated them, sending splinters of wood and fragments of bone flying like shrapnel.
BOOM. CRUNCH. SHATTER.

Every strike was calculated. Gorvasha wasn’t just killing; she was engineering. She would deliberately drive a knight backward, using the momentum of her hammer to slam him into specific sections of the corridor wall.

She knew exactly which stones were weakened, which supports were frayed, and which sections would collapse inward under a specific amount of force. She was fighting a battle and reshaping the battlefield simultaneously.
"Third rank, fall back six meters! "Gorvasha," she bellowed, her voice cutting through the cacophony of screams like a war horn. "Give them the gap!"
"Let them think they have won!"
"The stone will do the rest!"

As the Aethelgard soldiers rushed into the perceived opening, eager for a kill, Gorvasha slammed her hammer into the ground. The impact sent a shockwave through the floor that coordinated perfectly with the structural weaknesses she had spent weeks cultivating.
The corridor began to groan, the ancient stone weeping dust as it prepared to swallow the invaders whole.

chapters.title: Chapter 1142. Nothing Was Acknowledged, Because Acknowledgment Was a Luxury
paragraphs: While the front lines became a meat grinder of divine steel and demonic blood, Mordecai Vrael was fighting a different kind of war, a desperate, sweaty, terrified scramble for relevance.

He fought somewhere in the secondary rear formation, and frankly, he fought badly. If anyone had asked him honestly how he was doing, he would have admitted he was one bad swing away from becoming a stain on the cobblestones.
’Please work, please work, please God, just let something good come out of this stupid system,’ Mordecai screamed internally.
His hands were shaking so violently he could barely maintain the magical focus required to interface with the Infinite Gacha System. The air around him smelled of sulfur and panic.
"Come on! Give me something! Anything!" he shrieked, his voice cracking as an Aethelgard crossbow bolt whistled past his ear, embedding itself in the stone with a deadly thunk.

With a grunt of pure desperation, he triggered three summons in rapid succession. Three pillars of blinding gold light erupted across the rear formation, momentarily drowning out the crimson chaos of Cassandra’s massacre.
Through the haze of light, the units resolved: two SSR-ranked combatants materialized with a thunderous crash of displaced air, their armor gleaming with celestial authority.
Thanks to the residual energy Rex had been pumping into the battlefield; these weren’t just standard summons, they were juggernauts.

A third unit, a support class priestess, immediately planted her staff, casting a shimmering barrier that stabilized a section of the line that had been seconds away from collapsing under a barrage of enchanted arrows.
The summons tore into the Aethelgard advance with a ferocity that Mordecai could only dream of. They moved like living storms, their weapons carving through steel and bone with effortless cruelty.
Mordecai himself? He killed exactly two soldiers during the entire engagement.

Both times, it had been by complete accident: the first when he tripped and his dagger accidentally found a gap in a knight’s gorget, and the second when a stray magical discharge from one of his summons blew a soldier backward into his path.
’I’m going to die, I’m going to die, I’m going to die,’ his mind looped as an Aethelgard sergeant charged him, sword raised high.

Mordecai froze, eyes wide with terror, only for two Orc warriors to suddenly materialize between them. The Orcs didn’t say a word; they simply stepped into his space, their massive bodies forming a living wall that absorbed the sergeant’s blow.

They weren’t protecting him out of loyalty; they were protecting their summoner because if he died, the summons died. Mordecai didn’t notice; he just huddled behind them, breathing in ragged, terrified gasps.

In stark contrast to Mordecai’s shambolic terror, Pavellia Vostara moved through the mid formation like a lethal whisper. Where others were covered in gore and sweat, she remained eerily pristine, a vision of deadly elegance amidst the slaughter.
Fwish. Fwish. Fwish.
The sound of her feathers cutting through the air was almost musical. The iridescent plumage along her arms and back detached at her whim, transforming into razor-sharp projectiles.
Each feather found its mark with unerring accuracy: an eye socket here, a jugular there, and a gap in the visor there. She didn’t need to close the distance; she simply reaped from afar.
An Aethelgard squad attempted to close the gap on her, charging with shields raised. Pavellia didn’t even flinch.

With a subtle flick of her wrists, she sent a volley of feathers cascading downward. They didn’t just strike the soldiers; they carpeted the stone in front of her in a bristling field of deadly shafts.
The charging knights tripped over the makeshift barrier, their footing lost on the blood-slicked stone, and before they could recover, Pavellia’s next volley descended.
Thwack thwack thwack.
The feathers drove through flesh and bone like poisoned needles, pinning the fallen men to the ground.
"Hold the third formation."
"Three paces left... Close the gap," she commanded.
Her voice was quiet, crisp, and utterly devoid of the adrenaline-fueled screaming that defined the rest of the battle. Her subordinates obeyed instantly, moving like clockwork under her direction.
Behind his mask, Rex Rexilion watched her. He was calculating trajectories, energy expenditures, and casualty rates, but his attention kept drifting back to her.
His system, that omniscient, unerring tool that could read the deepest desires and darkest secrets of any living thing, had never once produced a reading for Pavellia Vostara.
He had scanned her countless times. He had looked for fear, for ambition, for hunger, for love.
But there was nothing. No number. No error message. No ’Null.’ It was as if the very concept of ’desire’ was a language she didn’t speak.
She existed outside the framework of need.

’What are you?’ Rex wondered, his eyes narrowing as he watched her pluck another feather from her wing to send it spiraling through a soldier’s throat. ’Are you even alive, or are you something else entirely wearing a human shape?’
It was a puzzle, a dangerous, profound anomaly in his perfect calculations. But as a fresh wave of Aethelgard cavalry thundered toward them, Rex pushed the thought aside.
He would solve her later. Right now, he had a war to win.
From the rear of the formation, Viscaria Amorphis conducted her symphony of gelatinous horror. The slime contingent was not merely a defensive line; they were a living, breathing counter spell.

Aethelgard’s mages unleashed torrents of concentrated fire and jagged ice magic, expecting to incinerate the rear ranks. Instead, the spells struck the translucent green mass of the slime soldiers and simply... vanished.
Sssssss Fwoosh.

The magical projectiles were swallowed whole. The slimes absorbed the energy with a contemptuous ease, their bodies rippling as they dissolved the spell structures on contact, only to reconstitute seconds later, thicker and more resilient than before.
Viscaria herself was a force of fluid devastation. When a concentrated barrage of enchanted crossbow bolts threatened to pierce the demon rear ranks, she threw her hands forward.
"Rise and shield!" she commanded, her voice echoing with a wet, gurgling undertone.

Massive liquid walls erupted from the ground, twenty meters across, surging upward to intercept the volley. The bolts struck the viscous barrier with wet thwips, embedding themselves harmlessly in the gelatinous mass.

But Viscaria fought with a new, guarded caution. Between each massive exertion of will, her hand would instinctively drift to the visible curve of her midsection, a subconscious gesture of protection that betrayed her altered priorities.

Twice, she deliberately pulled back from positions where she could have held the line with absolute certainty, choosing survival over martyrdom. She knew now that she was more valuable alive than as another splatter of gore on the corridor floor.
While Viscaria held the space, Lilith Nocturne owned the darkness.

Moving through the shadows at the corridor’s edge like smoke poured from a vial, Lilith was a ghost in the machinery of war. She was invisible to both armies, a predator watching prey that didn’t know she existed.
When two Nightwing scouts attempted to creep along a side seam toward a section of the corridor where Rex’s trap mechanisms were dangerously exposed, Lilith intervened.
She didn’t kill them yet. Instead, she leaned into the darkness, her lips curling into a cruel smile.
"Lost, little birds?" she whispered, though her voice was nothing more than a ripple in the air.
She wove a whispered succubus illusion across their minds. To the scouts, the corridor suddenly seemed familiar, safe, and already surveyed.

They turned around, walking confidently back toward their own lines, convinced they had already completed their mission. Lilith watched them go, her heart thrumming with a dark, intoxicating satisfaction.

She would never admit it, not even under the most exquisite torture, but she felt a fierce, possessive pride: Rex had trusted her with the unseen. He had given her the most dangerous job on the battlefield, and she was savoring every moment of it.

Yet, amidst the screaming metal and the wet sounds of slaughter, there were moments of eerie, unspoken connection moments that would never appear in any official war report because no one outside the immediate participants could possibly understand them.

High above on a jagged rock shelf, Talyra drew back her bowstring, the wood creaking ominously. Her target was a demon commander who was currently cleaving through an Aethelgard knight, sending a spray of arterial blood across the stones.
But as she lined up her shot, her sightline crossed directly with Cassandra Vexmoor’s.
For half a heartbeat, the two women locked eyes across the hellscape of the corridor. Talyra, the cold precision of the archer; Cassandra, the crimson fury of the Demon Queen.
Neither moved. No challenge was issued; no hostility was expressed. The air between them seemed to freeze, a silent acknowledgment of two predators operating in the same territory.
Then, as quickly as the connection formed, it shattered. Talyra shifted her aim to a different target with practiced indifference, and Cassandra turned her back to resume her butchery.
Nothing was acknowledged, because in this war, acknowledgment was a luxury they couldn’t afford.
A few meters away, the connection was even more visceral. Nerith thrust her hands toward the eastern wall, summoning a wall of thorned vines to trap a squad of Aethelgard soldiers.

As the green tendrils surged upward, she caught Gorvasha’s gaze. The Orc chieftain was watching her from twelve meters away, her face splattered with blood, her eyes burning with something that looked suspiciously like approval.
Nerith’s breath hitched. Her concentration wavered.
The vine wall she summoned came up three feet shorter than it should have, with a deliberate, almost imperceptible flaw.
"Now!" Gorvasha roared, though not to her own troops.

chapters.title: Chapter 1143. A Kill Zone Where Gravity Forgot Its Purpose
paragraphs: The gap in the vines allowed the Aethelgard soldiers to slip through, but Gorvasha’s immediate response was a calculated distraction.
She swung her massive warhammer downward, not at Nerith, but at a section of stone inches away from the druid’s feet.
BOOM.
The impact sent sparks and debris flying, creating a cloud of dust that masked Nerith’s retreat.
Both women turned away immediately afterward, their faces hardening into masks of war.
They never looked at each other again, but the unspoken pact hung between them like the scent of blood in the air: they were fighting two different wars, but they were fighting them together.
The battle raged on with a sickening, relentless momentum. The corridor had become a charnel house, a narrow throat of stone choking on the entrails and broken steel of two civilizations.
Bodies piled up in grotesque mounds, some still twitching from nerve damage, others already cooling in pools of spreading crimson.

On either side, the carnage was absolute. The wet slap of severed limbs hitting stone, the grinding screech of swords against bone, and the wet, gurgling pleas of dying men created a cacophony of horror.

Aethelgard’s forces were undeniably faster, their disciplined formations pushing with the momentum of a landslide, but that confidence, the divine certainty that had carried four thousand soldiers through the golden gateway, was beginning to fray.

The reality of the Underlayer was asserting itself like a vice. The narrow walls prevented their superior numbers from forming proper battle lines, turning their strength into a liability as they became packed too tightly to swing their weapons.
They weren’t an army anymore; they were a panicked herd being slaughtered in a tunnel.

’We’re trapped,’ a young Aethelgard squire thought, his eyes wide as he watched a demon claw rip through his captain’s breastplate, exposing the splintered ribs beneath with a wet crack. ’We’re all going to die in this godforsaken hole.’
And through all of it, through the screaming, the blood spray that painted the walls crimson, and the thunder of clashing steel, the masked figure at the exact center of the corridor had not moved.
He stood like a monument to stillness amidst a hurricane of violence, a black hole around which the chaos swirled but could not touch.
Then, he moved.
It was not a dramatic charge. There was no war cry, no sudden burst of speed, no theatrical flourish.
That was what unnerved the soldiers nearest to him more than any explosion could have. The masked figure simply took one step forward.
Then another. His gait was measured, unhurried, almost casual.
In the middle of a slaughterhouse where every second was a desperate scramble for survival, his calm was profoundly wrong.
It was wrong enough that several men on both sides, both demon and human, actually paused for a half beat, their weapons lowering instinctively as they stared at the walking anomaly.
’Why isn’t he fighting?’ an Aethelgard sergeant wondered, his heart hammering against his ribs. ’Why is he just... walking?’
Then, the mask began to glow.

It started as a faint tremor of color, a deep, bruised violet that seemed to bleed from the seams of the metal. It was dim at first, a low pulse like a dying heartbeat, but then it steadied, spreading outward from the edges of the mask.

The light washed over his shoulders, down his arms, and across his chest in a slow, deliberate bloom. This wasn’t the bright, hungry fire of a pyromancer; this was something colder. Something heavier.
Thrummm.
A low-frequency vibration began to emanate from the figure, a sound that wasn’t heard so much as felt in the marrow of one’s bones.
As the violet light intensified, the very atmosphere began to warp. The air in a twenty-meter radius around him suddenly seemed to thicken, turning from gas to something resembling liquid mercury.
The effect was immediate and terrifying. Soldiers who had been screaming battle cries found their voices dying in their throats.
The sound didn’t fade; it was smothered. The shouts became muffled gasps, then whispers, then nothing at all.
The air became dense and pressurized, as if the oxygen itself had been replaced by something far more potent and oppressive.
’I can’t... breathe...’ A demon warrior clawed at his own throat, feeling as though an invisible hand was pressing down on his lungs.
The space around the masked figure had ceased to be ordinary space. Gravity felt wrong; the light bent unnaturally around his silhouette.
The violet glow wasn’t just illuminating the corridor; it was claiming it. Every soldier within the radius felt the sudden, crushing realization that they weren’t standing in a battlefield anymore.
They were standing inside something else entirely. Something that had just woken up.
Cassandra Vexmoor saw it first. Through the spray of arterial blood and the haze of sulfurous smoke, that violet pulse cut through the chaos like a blade through silk.
Her pupils dilated as her instincts, the primal, ancient instincts of a Demon Queen who had survived countless eons, screamed a single warning: Get out.
Without breaking her stride, she disengaged from two Aethelgard knights she had been systematically dismantling.
One moment she was twisting a blade through a ribcage with a wet squelch; the next, she was executing six long, measured strides backward, her boots skidding on the gore-slicked stone.
"Fall back! Clear the center!" she commanded, her voice cracking like a whip over the din of slaughter.
Gorvasha caught the shift simultaneously. The Orc chieftain didn’t need to see the mask to know what it meant; she felt the change in atmospheric pressure before her eyes even registered the glow.
The hair on her neck stood on end. She bellowed a single, guttural roar to her warband, a sound that carried more authority than any tactical order.
"SHIFT! OPEN THE LANE! MOVE, YOU FOOLS!
The entire northern flank of the demon forces pivoted in unison, their massive bodies shifting their advance angle by twenty degrees.
They tore open a clear, empty lane through the center of the corridor, leaving a vacuum of space that seemed obscene amidst the crowding carnage.
Both women knew that glow. Both had witnessed the aftermath of that violet light on separate battlefields, each lesson paid for in screams and shattered bones.
Then, Xerollion walked into the Aethelgard formation.
The first man to challenge him was an elite household soldier, a veteran with eleven years of scarred experience who had earned a reputation for closing distance with lethal efficiency.
He saw the masked figure approaching and roared a battle cry, lunging forward with a blessed longsword aimed straight for the gap in the mask.
He never completed the swing.
CLANG BOOM!
Xerollion’s palm struck the soldier’s breastplate. The sound wasn’t the metallic ring of steel; it was the bone-deep reverberation of a sledgehammer hitting a cathedral bell.
The soldier’s momentum didn’t just stop; it reversed violently. His body launched backward with a speed the human mind couldn’t process, a blur of steel and screaming flesh.
He tore through three ranks of his own formation like a cannonball, his armored body crushing ribs with audible cracks and sending six soldiers tumbling like broken dolls.

Finally, he slammed into the corridor wall with such devastating force that the stone cratered inward, sending a cascade of dust and pebbles down. He slumped to the floor in a twisted heap, his armor crumpled inward where his chest cavity had been. He would never move again.
Then, the world began to break.
Vrrrrrrrrr...!
A low-frequency hum, almost subsonic, began to vibrate through the stone floor, shaking the teeth in every soldier’s skull.
In the same heartbeat that the soldier fell, Xerollion’s passive telekinetic field ignited. It wasn’t a targeted attack; it was an environmental takeover.
"What in the gods’ names—" an Aethelgard mage began, but his words were cut off by the sound of grinding stone.

Across a forty-meter stretch of the corridor floor, everything began to rise. Fallen swords, shattered spear shafts stained with blood, fist-sized chunks of broken masonry, and severed pieces of armor—everything lifted off the ground as if gravity had simply forgotten its purpose.
The debris rose slowly at first, then stabilized at chest height.
They did not fly at the enemy immediately. Instead, they hung there, suspended in a state of impossible stillness.
The weapons rotated slowly in the violet air, a suspended storm of jagged metal and razor-sharp rock. The ground around the masked figure was no longer a battlefield; it was a kill zone.

It was a cloud of suspended death that turned the corridor into a labyrinth where approaching from any direction meant navigating through a swirling vortex of debris that would decide, at Xerollion’s whim, whether to part like water or shred you like parchment.

chapters.title: Chapter 1144. A Demonstration of Absolute, Uncontested Dominion
paragraphs: The air in the corridor didn’t just feel heavy; it felt hostile. The violet haze surrounding Xerollion seemed to pulse in time with the grinding of teeth and the panicked breathing of the soldiers caught in his gravity well.
The suspended debris—shattered blades, jagged stone, and splintered bone—swirled in a lazy, hypnotic orbit that belied the lethal potential coiled within.
Then, the silence of the standoff shattered.
"For Aethelgard...! Strike now!" an officer screamed, his voice cracking with desperate bravado.
A squad of nine elite soldiers, veterans who had survived countless campaigns, made the attempt anyway.
They moved with the terrifying synchronization of a single organism, executing a coordinated collapse formation.

They hit him from four angles simultaneously, their shields overlapping, their weapons converging on the masked figure in a lethal pincer designed to overwhelm even the most powerful Apostle-ranked entities.
It was textbook, and it was flawless. But it was also a death sentence.
’Foresight.’
Inside the mind of the masked figure, time didn’t flow; it fractured. The next four seconds unfolded in layered, kaleidoscopic probabilities.

He saw every thrust before the muscle even twitched; he felt every shift in weight before the boot touched the stone. To him, the elite soldiers weren’t rushing forward; they were moving through molasses.
He moved. But he didn’t attack.
He simply... flowed.
The spearman charging from his left lunged with lethal intent, his spear tip aimed at the throat. Xerollion pivoted, a movement so minute it seemed almost lazy.
The spearhead tore through empty air, passing through the space where Xerollion’s neck had been a quarter second prior.

The momentum of the thrust was so great that the spearhead didn’t stop; it punched eighteen inches of consecrated steel through the shoulder of the swordsman closing from the front, the blade emerging from the man’s back in a spray of hot crimson.
Squelch CRACK.
The swordsman didn’t even have time to scream before his lungs filled with blood.
"What—no! Fall back, fall—" the spearman began, but his words died as the physics of the room turned against him.
The two soldiers closing from behind suddenly felt their own momentum inexplicably multiply. It was as if the air itself had grabbed them and flung them forward.

They hurtled past their target with terrifying speed, colliding with each other in the center with a wet, bone-crushing THUD that sent both crashing to the floor, unconscious before they even hit the stone.

A fifth soldier swung a massive warhammer in a desperate overhead arc, but as he committed to the strike, the gravity beneath his feet seemed to twist. His weapon missed Xerollion entirely, instead coming down with devastating force directly onto his own comrade’s spine.
The sound was unmistakable: the splintering of vertebrae like dry kindling breaking under a boot.
CRUNCH.
To any observer more than five meters away, it didn’t look like a fight. There was no clashing of steel, no heroic struggle.
It looked like a nightmare of impossible coincidences: a group of the finest soldiers in the realm suffering an inexplicable, catastrophic cascade of coordination failures.

Nine seconds after the engagement began, eight of them lay broken on the gore-slicked floor. The ninth, a young recruit whose eyes were wide with primal terror, turned and bolted, his boots slipping on the viscera of his fallen brothers.
What followed was not a battle. It was a demonstration of absolute, uncontested dominion.
A soldier, desperate to reclaim some shred of agency, attempted to sneak attack from behind. He lunged with a dagger, but mid-motion, his wrist was seized by an invisible force.
With a casual flick of intent, Xerollion snapped the radius and ulna backward.
CRACK.
The sound cut through the ambient noise of the war like a gunshot. Before the soldier’s scream could even escape his blood flecked lips, his entire body was hauled sideways by his own shattered arm.

He was swung like a human shield, his back slamming into a volley of arrows fired by his own panicked allies who were trying to hit the masked figure behind him. Three shafts buried themselves in his spine with three wet thwips.
Xerollion dropped the convulsing corpse without so much as glancing at it, moving on as if he had simply brushed aside a fly.
"Burn, you bastard!"
"Burn in the light of the gods!"

A battle mage, positioned twelve meters back behind a makeshift barrier of corpses, screamed her incantation. Her hands glowed with divine radiance as she completed a complex compound fire lance, a spell that required three seconds of precise channeling.
She watched with a flicker of savage satisfaction as the lance of superheated energy left her fingertips, streaking toward the violet haze.
She never saw it connect.
Mid-flight, the fire lance didn’t explode. It didn’t even slow down.
Energy manipulation caught the spell’s structure in midair, freezing the molten magical plasma. For a heartbeat, it hung there, quivering in the violet light.
Then, with a cruel twist of physics, the directional vector inverted. The spell didn’t just stop; it reversed, accelerating back toward its source with twice the velocity it had been launched with.
The mage’s eyes widened. "Oh=="
The fire lance struck her center mass. There was no prolonged struggle.

The superheated spell punched through her torso, cauterizing as it tore, leaving nothing but a smoking hole where her heart had been. Her scream was cut short by the sound of her own body collapsing into a charred heap.
Behind the impassive metal of his mask, Rex was savoring something sweeter than victory: he was savoring release.

For months, he had played the part of the mediocre student, pulling his punches in the Academy yards, deliberately faltering during tactical assessments, and stifling the monstrous potential of his body to avoid unwanted attention.

But here, amidst the copper tang of fresh blood and the screams of dying men, the shackles were off. His martial arts mastery and peak superhuman physique weren’t just tools; they were predators unleashed.
Every movement he made was terrifyingly economical. He didn’t waste energy on grand flourishes or heroic stances.

His motions were lazy, almost bored, yet each one ended with the wet thunk of a blade finding flesh or the sickening crunch of bone giving way. He moved like a predator that knew the prey had nowhere to run.
Roughly sixty seconds into his advance through the meat grinder, a figure emerged from the chaos that actually made Rex’s pulse quicken.
A captain of the elite guard.
This wasn’t some green recruit or a panicked conscript. This man moved with the terrifying grace of a seasoned killer.

His enchanted longsword hummed with residual holy energy, carving through the air with a whistle that cut through the din of battle. The captain launched into a masterwork combination of six flawless strikes that flowed together like liquid steel.
A high-line feint that demanded a parry, immediately followed by a low commitment that swept for the shins; a reverse cut that shifted elevation mid-swing with impossible fluidness.
This was a sequence honed through decades of bloodshed, a deadly dance designed to find the smallest gap in any opponent’s defense.
’Impressive,’ Rex thought, the words echoing in the private chamber of his mind. ’Let’s see how you handle real physics.’
Rex didn’t retreat. He didn’t even raise his hands to defend.

Instead, he performed a series of movements so minute they bordered on the insulting. A casual rotation of his left shoulder allowed the blade to whisper past his ear; a two-inch tilt of his head sent the next strike grazing his cheek without drawing blood.
He never stepped fully out of the sword’s reach, never breaking his stride. To step back would have been to acknowledge the captain as a threat.
To Rex, the Captain was merely an obstacle in motion.
On the seventh strike, a desperate, killing thrust aimed at the throat, Rex finally acted.
He didn’t block the sword. He reached out and caught the captain’s wrist.
CRACK SNAP.

The sound was sharp, like a dry branch breaking under immense pressure. With a single, brutal rotational snap, Rex folded the man’s wrist backward at an angle that defied human anatomy. Tendons frayed and bones shattered audibly.

The enchanted longsword clattered to the stone floor with a hollow metallic ring, abandoned by its master. Before the Captain’s first scream could even fully form in his throat, Rex’s palm connected with his sternum.
BOOM.
The strike landed with the force of a battering ram. The captain’s ribs didn’t just crack; they imploded, sending shards of bone inward toward his lungs.

The air was driven from his body in a spray of saliva and blood as he was lifted off his feet and slammed into the ground. He lay there, conscious and staring at the ceiling with pupils blown wide in shock, his chest cavity collapsed, breathing in wet, shallow gasps that sounded like drowning.
He was alive, but he was broken physically and spiritually beyond any hope of recovery.
Xerollion didn’t pause to gloat. He simply stepped over the convulsing officer and kept walking.
The psychological domino effect was instantaneous. The effect of his presence spread through the Aethelgard ranks faster than any commander’s order could stem.
These were men who had charged into this corridor forty minutes earlier with righteous fury, shouting hymns about justice for Veylor and Calivara.
Now, that fury had been replaced by something far more potent: primal terror.
