chapters.title: Chapter 1145. A Belief in Their Own Protection Died in That Moment
paragraphs: The psychological collapse of the Aethelgard forces was not a gradual retreat; it was a systemic failure. The formation didn’t just break it; it liquefied.

Men who had been prepared to die screaming hymns of divine justice moments before were now reduced to panicked animals, their boots scrabbling uselessly against the gore-slicked stone as they scrambled backward.

Their eyes, wide and bloodshot with terror, remained locked on the solitary masked figure, a walking catastrophe that had dismantled their finest elite in less time than it took to draw a full breath.
"Fall back to the flanks!"
"Disengage from the center immediately!" a high commander bellowed, his voice cracking like breaking glass as he witnessed the slaughter. "Redirect to the secondary lines!"
"Form a defensive perimeter around the archers!"
"MOVE, YOU COWARDS!"
On paper, the order was sound. It was a tactical concession meant to contain the anomaly by conceding the center ground.

But in the reality of the corridor’s claustrophobic confines, it was a catastrophic surrender. By attempting to avoid the meat grinder that was Xerollion, the soldiers were inadvertently creating a vacuum—a perfect, empty kill zone that Rex could dominate with terrifying ease.
He hadn’t just broken their line; he had hollowed out their entire strategy. He had been handed the heart of the battlefield on a silver platter, and he hadn’t even broken his stride to claim it.
Behind the cold metal of his mask, Rex inhaled deeply.

The air tasted of copper, burnt ozone, and fear. He could hear everything: the desperate shrieks of dying men, the wet slap of boots retreating, and the whimpering of soldiers who had finally realized they weren’t fighting a man, but something fundamentally alien.
’This is it,’ Rex thought, a dark chuckle echoing in the private theater of his mind. ’This is what it feels like to stop pretending.’

If anyone had been close enough to peer through the violet-lit slits of his mask, they would have seen something that would have frozen their blood: genuine, unadulterated delight dancing in his eyes. The adrenaline was a drug, more potent than any elixir the Academy could brew.
He pushed deeper.
Fifteen meters further into the Aethelgard formation, Rex reached the point of no return.

Here, the density of the retreating soldiers was so high that retreat had become a physical impossibility. The mass of armored bodies was jammed together, a human dam straining against the pressure of their own panic.
No matter what the commanders screamed, there was nowhere to go. They were trapped in a bottleneck of their own making.
Xerollion stopped.
The violet aura surrounding him suddenly intensified, bleeding outward like ink dropped into clear water.
He raised one hand, palm upward, fingers splayed as if grasping for something unseen. His fingers curled slightly, and Gravity Manipulation took hold with the wrath of a collapsing star.
"What is—? Why am I—" A soldier’s plea was cut off as his feet left the stone.
In a ten-meter radius around Rex, the world simply ceased to function.
Thirty-one soldiers were yanked from the ground simultaneously. There was no gradual lift, no feeling of rising; it was as if the earth itself had rejected them.

They rose six meters into the air in eerie, absolute silence. For two agonizing seconds, they hung there suspended in a state of impossible physics. Their weapons slipped from nerveless fingers, clattering uselessly against the walls.
Their bodies rotated slowly in the air, limbs flailing in a nauseating, disorienting spin that overrode every instinct of balance and survival their training had ever instilled.
The silence of the suspension was more terrifying than the noise of battle. It was the silence of the grave.

Some soldiers managed to scream high, thin sounds of pure existential horror, but most were too disoriented, their brains unable to process why the world had suddenly turned upside down. They hung there like meat suspended from hooks, helpless, vulnerable, and utterly doomed.
Xerollion’s fingers twitched. His eyes gleamed with cold amusement as he watched them dangle in his grasp.
Then, he released.
Gravity didn’t just return; it betrayed them.
In the span of a heartbeat, Rex inverted the gravitational constant. The suspension didn’t end with a gentle descent; it ended with a violent, crushing compression.
The thirty-one soldiers who had been floating like corpses in water were suddenly slammed downward by a force three times stronger than natural gravity.
CRUNCH SQUELCH.
The sound was catastrophic. It wasn’t the clatter of armor or the ring of steel; it was a single, wet, percussive explosion of breaking bone, bursting organs, and collapsing metal.
It sounded like thirty-one heavy sacks of meat being dropped from a tower onto concrete simultaneously.

The impact was so devastating that the stone floor of the corridor didn’t just receive them; it buckled, spiderwebbing outward in a radial pattern of shattered masonry that groaned under the sudden, impossible weight.
"Gods save us—" one soldier began, but his plea ended in a wet gurgle as his own ribcage collapsed inward, puncturing his lungs.

Most did not get up. Those who did didn’t stand; they convulsed, their limbs twisted at impossible angles, leaving trails of crimson smear across the cracked stone as they tried to crawl away from the carnage they had become.
Several would never walk again; their spines had been pulverized into something resembling gravel.
Rex watched through the violet haze, his breathing steady, his pulse a slow, rhythmic drumbeat of satisfaction.
’Physics is such a beautiful weapon,’ he mused.
But the Aethelgard forces weren’t finished. From the rear of the corridor, a contingent of battle mages, the last desperate hope of the remaining formation, began their incantations.
Their voices rose in a panicked, harmonized chant that reverberated off the walls.
"Shield of the Eternal Sun!"
"Bastion of Aethelgard!"
"Stand firm!"

They threw up three separate layers of defensive barriers, stacking them in the legendary ’Triple Tier’ configuration, the same magical architecture that had survived dragonfire during the Ignivara incident and repelled every siege the Legion had ever launched at Aethelgard’s walls.
Three concentric shells of shimmering gold and cerulean light formed a wall across the corridor’s width, a barrier designed to absorb, disperse, and nullify any known elemental threat.
Rex didn’t even flinch. He simply opened his palm, fingers curling as if grasping an invisible thread.
"Let’s try something new then," he whispered behind the mask.
Through Elemental Magic Creation, he unleashed a wave of energy. It wasn’t fire.
It wasn’t lightning. It was a phenomenon that had no name in any textbook in Erosyne, a searing, violet-black frequency of raw energy that defied every known taxonomy of magic.
The barriers didn’t shatter. They didn’t crack.
They simply... ceased to be.

The mages watched in frozen horror as their centuries-old defensive protocols encountered something their frameworks couldn’t even recognize. The barriers didn’t resist the wave; they dissolved from the outside inward, evaporating like mist before a supernova.
In less than a second, the ’impenetrable’ wall was gone, and the wave passed through the space where the barriers had been as if they had never existed.
Then, it hit the mages.
The scream that tore through the corridor was primal. The energy didn’t burn them so much as it unmade them, searing through their robes and flesh in an instant of incomprehensible agony.
The panic that followed was worse than the casualties. Soldiers could understand dying to a sword or even a fireball.

But watching three stacked, legendary barrier workings evaporate as though they were nothing more than decorative cobwebs broke something fundamental in the formation’s psyche. The belief in their own protection died in that moment.
The shouting spreading from that section of the line wasn’t tactical; it was the sound of men who had looked into the abyss and seen it smiling back.
"I-It’s not possible! "The barriers held against dragons!" someone shrieked, their voice cracking with genuine, soul-deep terror. "What is he? What IS HE?"
Rex didn’t give them time to answer. In the chaos of their terror, three soldiers, men who had decided that distance was their only remaining ally, hurled their spears at him simultaneously.
Three silver streaks cut through the smoke and blood, launched from three different angles with desperate, killing intent.

They threw up three separate layers of defensive barriers, stacking them in the legendary ’Triple Tier’ configuration, the same magical architecture that had survived dragonfire during the Ignivara incident and repelled every siege the Legion had ever launched at Aethelgard’s walls.
Three concentric shells of shimmering gold and cerulean light formed a wall across the corridor’s width, a barrier designed to absorb, disperse, and nullify any known elemental threat.
Rex didn’t even flinch.
He simply opened his palm, fingers curling as if grasping an invisible thread.
"Let’s try something new then," he whispered behind the mask.
Through Elemental Magic Creation, he unleashed a wave of energy.
It wasn’t fire.
It wasn’t lightning.
It was a phenomenon that had no name in any textbook in Erosyne, a searing, violet-black frequency of raw energy that defied every known taxonomy of magic.
The barriers didn’t shatter.
They didn’t crack.
They simply... ceased to be.
The mages watched in frozen horror as their centuries-old defensive protocols encountered something their frameworks couldn’t even recognize.
The barriers didn’t resist the wave; they dissolved from the outside inward, evaporating like mist before a supernova.
In less than a second, the ’impenetrable’ wall was gone, and the wave passed through the space where the barriers had been as if they had never existed.
Then, it hit the mages.
The scream that tore through the corridor was primal.
The energy didn’t burn them so much as it unmade them, searing through their robes and flesh in an instant of incomprehensible agony.
The panic that followed was worse than the casualties.
Soldiers could understand dying to a sword or even a fireball.
But watching three stacked, legendary barrier workings evaporate as though they were nothing more than decorative cobwebs broke something fundamental in the formation’s psyche.
The belief in their own protection died in that moment.
The shouting spreading from that section of the line wasn’t tactical; it was the sound of men who had looked into the abyss and seen it smiling back.
"I-It’s not possible!
"The barriers held against dragons!" someone shrieked, their voice cracking with genuine, soul-deep terror.
"What is he?
What IS HE?"
Rex didn’t give them time to answer.
In the chaos of their terror, three soldiers, men who had decided that distance was their only remaining ally, hurled their spears at him simultaneously.
Three silver streaks cut through the smoke and blood, launched from three different angles with desperate, killing intent.

chapters.title: Chapter 1146. Fear Makes Men Run, Martyrdom Makes Them Unbreakable
paragraphs: The three spears streaked through the smoke-choked air like silver lightning, each aimed at a different vital point: throat, heart, and groin. To any other warrior, it would have been a fatal triangulation, a coordinated execution attempt.
But Rex didn’t move to dodge. He didn’t even flinch.
Instead, he extended his right hand. He didn’t grasp the shafts; he seized the space around them.
A micro thin layer of molecular precision telekinesis snapped into existence, creating an invisible cage of force that intercepted all three projectiles mid-flight.
VROOOOM THUD.

The spears stopped dead in midair, millimeters from his mask, frozen in time. They hung there, quivering violently against the unseen barrier, the kinetic energy of the throw still rippling through the wood.

Rex stared at them with the detached, clinical interest of a scientist examining a specimen under a microscope. He analyzed their vectors, their velocity, and the desperation etched into their trajectories.
’Too predictable,’ he thought. ’Too emotional.’
’You’re throwing away your lives like they’re worthless.’
’Let me show you what happens when you actually waste something precious.’

With a flick of his wrist, a motion as casual as shooing away a fly, he reversed the momentum. The telekinetic force didn’t just push them back; it amplified their speed by a factor of five, sending them shrieking back toward their owners with devastating force.
SHRAK THWIP!

The first thrower didn’t even have time to gasp before his own spear punched through his left thigh, splintering the femur with a sound like a gunshot. He collapsed instantly, screaming a wet, ragged sound as blood geysered from the wound, painting the cracked stone crimson.
SQUELCH.
The second spear found its mark with unerring accuracy, driving through his right shoulder and embedding itself three inches deep into the wall behind him.
The man was pinned to the masonry like an insect in a display case, his face draining of color as he hung there, convulsing in shock.

The third soldier, perhaps blessed by some distant deity, managed to twist his torso at the last possible microsecond. The spear missed his sternum but tore through the thick meat of his upper arm, ripping through muscle fibers and tendons.
He fell to his knees, clutching the ruined limb, his breath coming in desperate, sobbing gasps. It was a mercy, a calculated, precise adjustment in Rex’s internal equation.
This wasn’t cruelty. It wasn’t even sadism.
To Rex, this was simply arithmetic.
’Kill enough to break the assault,’ he reasoned, his mind working with terrifying coldness. ’But not enough to create a legend of invincibility that demands a hero.’
’If they think I am a god, they will fight with martyrdom.’
’If they think I am a monster, they will fight with fear.’
’Fear is more useful. Fear makes men run.’
’Men who run can be hunted. Men who die as martyrs become unbreakable.’
He needed to maintain the illusion of being a man, a very dangerous, very lethal man, but not a supernatural inevitability.
Cripple where possible.
Disable where necessary.
Terrify always.
Kill only when the math demanded it.
The difference would matter enormously when this war’s official history was written by the very people who would eventually trust him.
The slaughter was becoming too loud, too messy. It was time to change the texture of the battlefield.
Rex reached into the darkest recesses of his power: Sovereign Necromancy.
He didn’t unleash it in a torrent of bone and shadow; he used it like a scalpel. He drew just enough essence from the recently deceased to twist their lingering echoes back into the world.
Rrrrrip... Shhhhh.
Eleven corpses began to stir from the blood-slicked floor. They rose in a loose, unnatural arc across the front of his advance.
These weren’t the theatrical, snarling zombies of folklore. There were no glowing eyes, no roars of rage.
They rose with the slack, hollow posture of marionettes whose strings had been cut and reattached by an amateur. They stood with empty sockets staring at nothing, their skin a pale, bruised grey.
They did not attack. Rex had not given them that command.
Instead, they simply... walked.
A slow, relentless, shambling advance that cut through the chaos like a cold fog. Each step they took toward the living soldiers was accompanied by the wet slap of dead feet on gore-soaked stone.
"Stay back! Get away from them!" a sergeant screamed, but his voice lacked conviction.
His sword hand was shaking so violently the blade rattled against his shield.
The psychological weight was unbearable. The living soldiers found themselves unable to maintain their formation.
How do you charge into a line when the front rank consists of your own dead friends?
How do you thrust a spear through a man whose face you recognized from the mess hall only yesterday?
"I can’t... I can’t do this..." A young recruit whimpered, dropping his shield with a clang that sounded like a death knell.
He turned and bolted into the darkness behind the lines.

Another soldier, a seasoned veteran who had survived three campaigns, suddenly doubled over, retching violently onto the floor as his stomach rebelled against the sight of his fallen comrade walking toward him with a vacant, eyeless stare. He couldn’t even lift his weapon.

The corridor’s central advance, the backbone of Aethelgard’s desperate push, disintegrated. In under twenty seconds, a disciplined military unit had dissolved into a panicked mass of terrified individuals.
And the most terrifying part? Not one of Rex’s constructs had landed a single blow.
They simply existed as a reminder that even death was now under his command.

Beneath the reinforced soles of Rex’s boots, something far more insidious than brute force was at work. His Earthen Divine Authority ran in a continuous, silent loop, bleeding into the very foundation of the corridor.
To the Aethelgard soldiers, the floor appeared unchanged; the stone was still cold, still solid, still gray. But physics itself was being subtly sabotaged.
Every step Rex took sent an imperceptible harmonic resonance through the substrate of the corridor. Within a fifteen-meter radius of his position, the world became treacherous.
It wasn’t that the ground shook; it was that the ground became uncooperative. A soldier attempting to pivot would find his footing yielding by a fraction of a millimeter too far.
A commander trying to plant his sword for a thrust would find the resistance lacking, his weight transfer sluggish and imprecise.
Thump... Thump... Thump...
Each of Rex’s footsteps felt like a heartbeat echoing through the earth. Inside that field, the Aethelgard formation was fighting a war against their own momentum.

To them, it felt as though the air had thickened into syrup, as though every movement required an exhausting expenditure of effort. From Rex’s perspective, they moved like drowning men desperate, flailing, and fatally slow.
’Left flank is staggering,’ Rex noted, his mind processing the battlefield as a series of failing equations. ’Their reaction times have dropped by approximately twelve percent... Perfect.’
Then, the pressure changed. The ambient noise of screams and clattering armor fell away as a new, sharper magical signature pierced through the chaos.
An apostle had arrived.
Rex didn’t know his name. He wouldn’t learn it, nor would he care.
The man was a mid-tier asset in the divine network, drawing power from one of the lesser pantheon deities. By mortal standards, he was a walking catastrophe.

His magic wasn’t a crude fireball or a physical blade; he wielded a binding structure that operated on the soul’s adjacent register, a metaphysical tether designed to lock a target’s essence in place before they could even think to defend themselves.
The Apostle charged through the panicked ranks, his eyes blazing with holy fervor. "By the Light of the Third Throne, I bind you, demon—!"
Rex’s Divine Perception flickered to life. In the microsecond before the Apostle’s hands even formed the spell, Rex saw it.

He didn’t just see the magic; he saw its blueprint. He saw the way the energy braided together, the way it sought to anchor itself to the soul’s frequency, and the exact mathematical structure of the binding spell.
It was like reading an open book written in glowing ink.
’Interesting,’ Rex thought. ’A soul anchor.’
’High complexity, low adaptability. Let’s see how it handles a perfect counter.’
Full Potential Adaptation engaged instantly.
The Apostle unleashed the spell. A burst of prismatic light erupted from his palms, rushing toward Rex like a coiled serpent seeking to constrict.
The spell struck. For half a heartbeat, Rex felt a strange, phantom tightening across his very essence, a ghostly pressure that suggested his soul was being grasped by invisible hands.
But then, the analysis was completed.
The adaptation protocols wrapped around Rex’s spiritual signature like a flawless armor. The binding spell reached him, found no purchase, and simply... unraveled.
The intricate magical weave didn’t shatter; it dissolved. The energy bled away into nothingness, torn apart at the molecular level as if a loose thread had been pulled from a piece of silk.
The Apostle froze. The prismatic light died in his hands.
The silence that followed was more deafening than the battle raging around them.
Rex watched the man’s face. It was a masterpiece of psychological collapse.
In two seconds, a decade of religious certainty, years of training, and the entire identity of a divine warrior evaporated.

The Apostle’s eyes went wide, pupils contracting as he stared at his own hands, then at Rex, then at the empty air where his greatest weapon should have been. The realization that he wasn’t just outmatched and that he was fundamentally irrelevant was worse than any wound.
"How..." the Apostle whispered, his voice cracking, stripped of all divine authority. "How can you... how is this possible?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1147. I Was Wondering How Long It Would Take You
paragraphs: Rex took a single step forward. The ground beneath him hummed with restrained power.
The violet glow of his mask seemed to pulse brighter.
"Practice," Xerollion said, his voice flat and utterly devoid of empathy.
Rex didn’t use magic for the finishing blow. He didn’t need to.
He simply stepped into the man’s space and delivered a single, controlled strike across his jaw.
CRACK.
The sound of the mandible breaking was sharp and clean. The Apostle’s head snapped sideways with inhuman force, his brain bouncing against the inside of his skull.
He didn’t even have time to register the pain before consciousness fled. His body went limp, collapsing into the blood-soaked stone like a marionette whose strings had been cut.
Rex didn’t pause to check his pulse. He simply stepped over the fallen divine warrior and continued his advance into the heart of the slaughter.
Rex straightened his spine, the motion slow and deliberate, as if he were merely shaking off the dust of a long day rather than standing in the center of a slaughterhouse.
He took a long, measured breath, letting the metallic tang of blood and the acrid stench of scorched magic fill his lungs.
The corridor was unrecognizable. Six minutes ago, it had been a disciplined artery of golden armor and righteous purpose; now, it was a charnel house.
The central formation of Aethelgard hadn’t just broken; it had been pulverized. Over a fifty-meter stretch of stone, the floor was carpeted in human debris.
Bodies lay twisted at impossible angles, their armor shattered and their flesh torn.

The overwhelming majority were either unconscious from shock and concussive force or too broken to move, men with shattered femurs protruding through leather, men whose ribs had been crushed inward by gravitational spikes, leaving them gasping wetly through punctured lungs.
Crunch. Slosh.
Every step Rex took produced a sickening sound as his boots pressed into the congealing mixture of blood and viscera that now coated the stones.

The survivors, those few who still possessed the will to hold a weapon, had retreated with desperate, animalistic terror. They had pulled back toward the walls so far that the entire central span of the corridor now belonged to a single man.

The tactical formation was gone; there was only a terrified hollow circle around the predator. Field commanders were screaming retreat orders, their voices cracking with a hysteria that betrayed their loss of control.
"Fall back! To the secondary gates!"
"Break formation and run!" a captain shrieked, but the order was redundant.
The men were already fleeing, their boots slipping on the gore as they scrambled toward the flanks, abandoning their posts, their honor, and their comrades.
The momentum that had carried four thousand sanctified warriors through a golden gateway hadn’t just stalled; it had reversed with the violence of a collapsing star.
Rex watched them flee through the slit of his mask.
’Panic is the most honest emotion,’ he thought. ’No lies in it.’
’No dogma... Just the raw, naked terror of realizing you are prey.’
Apollo Brightsoul finally felt it far up the corridor, where the remaining disciplined elements of the vanguard still clung to their positions like drowning rats.
The commander of the Aethelgard forces froze. A coldness that had nothing to do with the ambient temperature crept up his spine.

He was mid-sentence, barking orders to reinforce the left flank, when the silence from behind him became too loud. The absence of the rhythmic march and the absence of the shouting—it was a vacuum that screamed of catastrophe.
Apollo turned. His golden armor glinted under the magical lighting of the corridor, but his face was pale.

His eyes swept across the wreckage, taking in the carnage that stretched back like a trail of broken promises. He saw the bodies, the blood, the shattered divine barriers, and the hollowed-out remains of his army.
Then, his gaze locked onto the source.
In the dead center of the devastation stood Rex. He was the eye of the storm.
Amidst the twisted metal, the broken bones, and the spreading crimson pools, Rex appeared preternaturally clean.
His breathing was steady, his posture relaxed, not a single scratch marring his gear. He looked less like a soldier and more like an inevitability.
Rex didn’t raise a weapon. He didn’t cast a spell.
He simply turned his head with agonizing slowness until his masked gaze found Apollo’s across the vast, blood-slicked distance.
The two men stared at each other across a wasteland of their own making. The air between them seemed to vibrate with the residual tension of a thousand dying screams.
Rex waited. He didn’t need to move.
He simply stood there, a silent sentinel in the ruins, letting the horror of what he had done sink into Apollo’s soul, waiting for the commander to realize that the real fight had only just begun.
Apollo disengaged from the front line the moment the implications of the carnage crystallized in his mind. The tactical reality was no longer about pushing forward; it was about survival.
"Elliot!" Apollo’s voice cracked like a whip as he seized his lieutenant’s shoulder mid-swing, spinning him around with enough force to stagger him. "The center..."
"Listen to me carefully... Take command of the forward push!"
"Hold this line at all costs, but do not under any circumstances advance past that stone ridge."
"Do you understand? That is an order!"
Elliot stumbled back, his sword lowering as his eyes followed Apollo’s frozen gaze down the corridor. The lieutenant’s face drained of color beneath layers of dried blood and battlefield grime.
"Apollo..." he whispered, his voice trembling. "Gods above, that’s how many of them are down?"
"That’s got to be three hundred people... Three hundred gone in minutes."
"Hold the line," Apollo repeated, his jaw working silently. "That is all I need from you."
Then, he began to move.

His pace was not the confident stride of a commander leading a charge; it was the measured, agonizingly cautious approach of an apex predator that had stumbled into the territory of something far more dangerous.
Every muscle in Apollo’s body was coiled tight, his instincts screaming at him that the man standing in the distance was not a soldier but a catastrophe given human form.
With every step Apollo took, the golden light of his affinity began to hemorrhage from his pores. It bled through his armor, coating his shoulders and forearms in a corona of divine radiance.

The light grew brighter, more desperate, casting long, dancing shadows against the gore-stained walls. By the time he came to a halt ten meters short of the masked figure, the corridor was flooded with a warm, artificial dawn.
Rex had not moved an inch. He remained a statue of obsidian and violet, standing precisely where he had been when Apollo first spotted him.

He stood amidst the broken bodies as if they were nothing more than fallen leaves in a courtyard, waiting with the terrifying patience of someone who had already won the game before the first move was made.

Apollo’s eyes swept the battlefield one last time. His gaze lingered on the crumpled form of a young spearman whose throat had been torn open, then on a veteran sergeant whose legs had been twisted into unnatural positions.
These were not just casualties; these were names. These were men and women Apollo had trained, men and women whose families he had promised protection to.
He had stood on marble platforms and spoken of divine necessity, and now he stood in the crimson reality of his own failure.
When he finally spoke, the anger that came out was not a roar; it was something worse. It was a low, vibrating fury that shook his entire frame.
"You did all of this," Apollo said, each word dripping with venomous accusation.
Rex tilted his head slightly.
"Be more specific," he countered.
His voice was flat, utterly unburdened by the weight of the corpses surrounding him.
"Not just here." Apollo’s hands clenched into fists so tight his gauntlets creaked ominously. "All of it..."
"The Undead Bringer."
"The tremor that shattered the northern provinces."
"The dragon that burned the eastern settlements."
"You are behind every single one of them... Every drop of blood spilled in this war traces back to your hands."

A ghost of a smile seemed to touch the air around Rex’s mask. The reply came with a calm, almost mild cadence, the tone of a tutor mildly disappointed in a student who had failed to grasp a simple concept.
"I was wondering how long it would take you." Rex said, stepping over the twitching corpse of a fallen guard without breaking eye contact. "Though I can’t say I’m surprised it took this long."
"You’ve always been far too busy trusting the people around you to actually look at what’s standing directly in front of you."

The men were already fleeing, their boots slipping on the gore as they scrambled toward the flanks, abandoning their posts, their honor, and their comrades.
The momentum that had carried four thousand sanctified warriors through a golden gateway hadn’t just stalled; it had reversed with the violence of a collapsing star.
Rex watched them flee through the slit of his mask.
’Panic is the most honest emotion,’ he thought. ’No lies in it.’
’No dogma...
Just the raw, naked terror of realizing you are prey.’
Apollo Brightsoul finally felt it far up the corridor, where the remaining disciplined elements of the vanguard still clung to their positions like drowning rats.
The commander of the Aethelgard forces froze.
A coldness that had nothing to do with the ambient temperature crept up his spine.
He was mid-sentence, barking orders to reinforce the left flank, when the silence from behind him became too loud.
The absence of the rhythmic march and the absence of the shouting—it was a vacuum that screamed of catastrophe.
Apollo turned.
His golden armor glinted under the magical lighting of the corridor, but his face was pale.
His eyes swept across the wreckage, taking in the carnage that stretched back like a trail of broken promises.
He saw the bodies, the blood, the shattered divine barriers, and the hollowed-out remains of his army.
Then, his gaze locked onto the source.
In the dead center of the devastation stood Rex.
He was the eye of the storm.
Amidst the twisted metal, the broken bones, and the spreading crimson pools, Rex appeared preternaturally clean.
His breathing was steady, his posture relaxed, not a single scratch marring his gear.
He looked less like a soldier and more like an inevitability.
Rex didn’t raise a weapon.
He didn’t cast a spell.
He simply turned his head with agonizing slowness until his masked gaze found Apollo’s across the vast, blood-slicked distance.
The two men stared at each other across a wasteland of their own making.
The air between them seemed to vibrate with the residual tension of a thousand dying screams.
Rex waited.
He didn’t need to move.
He simply stood there, a silent sentinel in the ruins, letting the horror of what he had done sink into Apollo’s soul, waiting for the commander to realize that the real fight had only just begun.
Apollo disengaged from the front line the moment the implications of the carnage crystallized in his mind.
The tactical reality was no longer about pushing forward; it was about survival.
"Elliot!" Apollo’s voice cracked like a whip as he seized his lieutenant’s shoulder mid-swing, spinning him around with enough force to stagger him.
"The center..."
"Listen to me carefully...
Take command of the forward push!"
"Hold this line at all costs, but do not under any circumstances advance past that stone ridge."
"Do you understand?
That is an order!"
Elliot stumbled back, his sword lowering as his eyes followed Apollo’s frozen gaze down the corridor.
The lieutenant’s face drained of color beneath layers of dried blood and battlefield grime.
"Apollo..." he whispered, his voice trembling.
"Gods above, that’s how many of them are down?"
"That’s got to be three hundred people...
Three hundred gone in minutes."
"Hold the line," Apollo repeated, his jaw working silently.
"That is all I need from you."
Then, he began to move.

His pace was not the confident stride of a commander leading a charge; it was the measured, agonizingly cautious approach of an apex predator that had stumbled into the territory of something far more dangerous.
Every muscle in Apollo’s body was coiled tight, his instincts screaming at him that the man standing in the distance was not a soldier but a catastrophe given human form.
With every step Apollo took, the golden light of his affinity began to hemorrhage from his pores.
It bled through his armor, coating his shoulders and forearms in a corona of divine radiance.
The light grew brighter, more desperate, casting long, dancing shadows against the gore-stained walls.
By the time he came to a halt ten meters short of the masked figure, the corridor was flooded with a warm, artificial dawn.
Rex had not moved an inch.
He remained a statue of obsidian and violet, standing precisely where he had been when Apollo first spotted him.

He stood amidst the broken bodies as if they were nothing more than fallen leaves in a courtyard, waiting with the terrifying patience of someone who had already won the game before the first move was made.
Apollo’s eyes swept the battlefield one last time.
His gaze lingered on the crumpled form of a young spearman whose throat had been torn open, then on a veteran sergeant whose legs had been twisted into unnatural positions.
These were not just casualties; these were names.
These were men and women Apollo had trained, men and women whose families he had promised protection to.
He had stood on marble platforms and spoken of divine necessity, and now he stood in the crimson reality of his own failure.
When he finally spoke, the anger that came out was not a roar; it was something worse.
It was a low, vibrating fury that shook his entire frame.
"You did all of this," Apollo said, each word dripping with venomous accusation.
Rex tilted his head slightly.
"Be more specific," he countered.
His voice was flat, utterly unburdened by the weight of the corpses surrounding him.
"Not just here." Apollo’s hands clenched into fists so tight his gauntlets creaked ominously.
"All of it..."
"The Undead Bringer."
"The tremor that shattered the northern provinces."
"The dragon that burned the eastern settlements."
"You are behind every single one of them...
Every drop of blood spilled in this war traces back to your hands."
A ghost of a smile seemed to touch the air around Rex’s mask.
The reply came with a calm, almost mild cadence, the tone of a tutor mildly disappointed in a student who had failed to grasp a simple concept.
"I was wondering how long it would take you." Rex said, stepping over the twitching corpse of a fallen guard without breaking eye contact.
"Though I can’t say I’m surprised it took this long."
"You’ve always been far too busy trusting the people around you to actually look at what’s standing directly in front of you."

chapters.title: Chapter 1148. The Same Man He Had Trusted More Completely Than Anyone Alive
paragraphs: Apollo’s entire body trembled. It wasn’t the involuntary shake of terror, but something far more volatile: the violent, convulsive effort of a man restraining a hurricane.
His muscles were locked in a state of hypertension, his tendons standing out like steel cables beneath his skin as he fought the primal urge to simply lunge forward and tear Rex apart.

Rex watched that restraint with a detached, clinical fascination. Through the violet lenses of his mask, he could see the minute physiological tells: the rapid dilation of Apollo’s pupils and the erratic rhythm of his pulse visible in the carotid artery of his neck.

He wasn’t just watching a man; he was watching a dam about to burst. More interesting than the physical confrontation would be the psychological one: the slow, agonizing structural collapse of a worldview that had been built on the comforting assumption that the universe possessed some form of inherent justice.
"Veylor," Apollo began, his voice rising, cracking with the sheer volume of the grief and rage building in his chest. "Calivara... Eryndra... How many more, Xerollion...?"
"How many others have you butchered with your own hands while standing beside us?"
"How many times have you played the part of the concerned ally, pretending to be another victim of the same chaos you orchestrated?!"
"A fair number." The reply was immediate.
No hesitation. No flicker of guilt. Just a flat statement of fact, as dispassionate as a ledger entry.
"I’m not going to stand here and recite a death toll for your comfort, Apollo..."
"It isn’t what I came here for..."
"What I’m actually interested in is what you intend to do now that the illusion has been stripped away."
Apollo took a step forward. Then another.

The distance between them closed until only a few meters remained, and then the atmosphere itself seemed to ignite. The two opposing auras, Apollo’s searing, righteous gold and Rex’s cold, implacable violet, collided in the space between them.
The air grew heavy, charged with static that made the hair on Apollo’s arms stand on end. The pressure was physical, a tangible weight that pushed against their chests like the depths of an ocean.
Ssssss...
The sound of magical energy crackling between them filled the corridor like the hiss of steam.
"You killed the people I loved," Apollo said. His voice had dropped.

The shouting had ceased, replaced by something infinitely more dangerous: a quiet, focused hatred that carried more killing intent than any battle cry. "You destroyed the lives of people I swore to protect with every fiber of my being."
"You made Theo into—"
He stopped abruptly. His jaw locked so tightly that the bone seemed to strain against the skin. The name hung in the air between them like a poisoned blade.
"Theo wasn’t mine."

The interruption came from Rex, and for the first time, the calm facade slipped. A sharper edge entered his voice—not anger, but a cold, cutting precision that sliced through Apollo’s emotional outburst.

"Theo was the product of his own choices and a desperate god who found a broken young man at the bottom of a cliff and offered him a weapon," Rex said, stepping forward to meet Apollo’s gaze, refusing to let the commander dominate the space. "I merely happened to be standing at the end of a sequence of failures he had been assembling for months before I ever became relevant to his story."
Rex’s violet aura flared momentarily, casting jagged shadows across the blood-slick floor. "If you want to assign blame for Theo’s fate, Apollo, don’t waste your breath on me."
"Start with the household that stripped him of his dignity and the god who caught him on his way down just to use him as a blade."
"I didn’t break him... I simply watched as he shattered himself."

Rex began walking forward as he spoke. His stride was slow, almost casual, the measured pace of a man strolling through a private garden rather than closing the final meters toward a confrontation that would likely end in mutual annihilation.

Behind the obsidian surface of his mask, Rex was savoring the spectacle. He drank in every minute flicker of rage that contorted Apollo’s features, each twitch of his jaw and each desperate pulse in his throat.

That dormant part of his psyche, the part that had never required a strategic justification for cruelty, had surfaced in full, now neatly concealed behind a calm timbre and the soft, violet glow of his visor.

"Do you want to know what I find most interesting about this, Apollo?" Rex tilted his head slightly, examining his opponent like a specimen under glass. "You’re standing there trying to understand the reasoning behind everything that has been done to you."
"You’re searching for some grand design, some twisted logic underneath the carnage that would make all of it easier to carry once you finally uncovered it."
A cold chuckle rumbled in Rex’s chest. "There isn’t."
"There was never going to be... I did all of this because I could, and because I enjoyed watching the light leave their eyes."
Something inside Apollo didn’t just crack; it detonated.

The golden light surrounding Apollo erupted outward in a cataclysmic shockwave. It was a corona of divine fury that surpassed anything he had displayed during the plaza fight against Tremor, eclipsing the power he had summoned against Theo.

The radiance climbed to such an impossible intensity that several soldiers watching from forty meters back had to scream and dive for cover, raising their armored arms to shield their eyes from the searing brilliance.

The air around Apollo began to taste like the ionized copper inside a lightning storm. When he finally raised his gaze to meet the mask, his eyes were gone, replaced by two twin suns of pure, molten gold.
"I don’t care about your reasons anymore," Apollo said.

The divine resonance in his voice had grown so potent that the words didn’t seem to come from his throat alone; they vibrated out of the stone walls, the corpses, and the very air itself. "I only care about making certain you never hurt another living person after today."
Behind the mask, Rex smiled. No one could see it, but the shift in his stance made it unmistakable.

He spread both arms slightly outward, not in a defensive guard, but as an invitation. His entire body filled with the coiled, hungry anticipation of a predator that had finally found prey worth the effort of playing with before the slaughter begins.
There was no fear in him. There had not been fear in his soul for a very long time.
"Very well then," Xerollion whispered.

His voice dropped to a low, satisfied murmur that somehow carried across the entire stretch of the ruined corridor, cutting through the crackling static of their clashing auras. "Show me what an Apostle of Life can do once he’s lost everything."
The silence between them held for exactly one heartbeat, a suspended moment of absolute stillness where even the blood dripping from the ceiling seemed to freeze midair.
BOOM.
Then Apollo moved. He became a streak of golden lightning, roaring off his body in a blaze that ignited the corridor from wall to wall.
The sound of his boots hitting the stone was like thunderclaps, each step sending cracks spiderwebbing through the blood-slicked floor.
Rex met him halfway, moving not with desperation, but with something approximating joy.

The world narrowed down to a single point of collision. On one side, the hero who had spent months bleeding, grieving, and sacrificing for a city he loved; on the other, the enemy who stood in his way, the man who, though Apollo would not learn it in this corridor, or perhaps for a very long time afterward, was the same man he had trusted more completely than anyone else alive.

chapters.title: Chapter 1149. How Many Things I Believed Absolute Truths Died Five Minutes Ago
paragraphs: Apollo crossed the distance in a single, explosive movement. He didn’t just run; he became a projectile of divine wrath, his boots tearing gouges into the stone as he accelerated.
But the corridor answered before his fist could even find flesh.
CRACK BOOM!
The punch connected with the empty space where the masked figure had been standing a fraction of a second earlier, but there was no empty air.

Rex had moved with a preternatural fluidity that defied human reaction time. When Apollo’s fist missed, the golden light wrapped around his knuckles didn’t simply dissipate; it detonated against the air itself.
The shockwave rolled outward from the point of impact in a visible, searing ring of compressed dust and displaced light.

The force was so immense that it acted like a physical wall; the nearest soldiers on both sides were lifted off their feet as if struck by a battering ram, forty or fifty men tumbling backward into the corpses of their comrades.
The sound that followed was a bone-deep roar that slammed into the corridor walls and ricocheted back three times over, leaving a ringing silence in its wake that felt heavier than the noise itself.
Across a hundred meters of passage, the war simply stopped. Soldiers froze mid-swing, their blades suspended in the air.
They hadn’t made a tactical decision to cease fire; their primal instincts had simply overridden their training.

Their bodies had registered something at the center of the corridor that belonged to an entirely different category of existence, something that made their struggle for territory feel like children playing with wooden swords.
Hands loosened on sword hilts; armor rattled as men instinctively took half steps back. All eyes turned toward the epicenter of the devastation.
Twenty meters away from the chaos, Valentina Von Starlight had stopped casting entirely.
Her fingers, still stained with the residue of arcane channeling, twitched at her sides.
She had spent the last hour holding this retreat corridor with complex workings that would have drained three Academy mages to exhaustion, but she abandoned every spell the moment the duel ignited.
Her breathing was shallow as she witnessed something that violated every fundamental law of magical theory she had ever studied.

She watched with horrified fascination as the masked figure slipped a strike that should have been physically impossible to evade. She saw him twist his torso with impossible economy, finding a window of opportunity that lasted perhaps a tenth of a second, a gap so small it shouldn’t have existed, and counter with a precision that felt more like surgery than combat.

Her mind, trained by years of ruthless academic discipline, began to frantically build a mental profile of this combatant. His capability set didn’t just exceed the Apostle network’s records; it rendered them obsolete.
’This isn’t a fight,’ she thought, a cold sweat breaking out across her brow. ’This is a collision of fundamental forces.’
"Headmaster." One of her lieutenants appeared at her shoulder, his voice cracking with uncertainty. "Orders? We need to support Apollo before
"Hold position." Valentina’s voice was flat, cutting through the lieutenant’s panic like a guillotine blade. "Nobody advances."
"That is an absolute order!"
"But Apollo is fighting for our lives! If we don’t push—"
"I am well aware of what Apollo is doing," Valentina snapped, her eyes never wavering from the golden and violet flashes erupting in the distance.

She watched a gout of golden flame erupt from the center, followed immediately by a shockwave of violet energy that shattered a nearby stone pillar into fine powder. "If we send soldiers into that space, they won’t be reinforcements."
"They will become debris... We hold position and we pray."

Morwenna Nightwing arrived beside Valentina only minutes later. Her breathing was ragged, with each inhale producing a sharp hiss through her clenched teeth, and the dark blood spattered across her silver gauntlets was clearly not her own.

She took one look at the apocalyptic display unfolding at the corridor’s center—the searing flashes of gold and violet that made the very air tremble and fell silent. For Morwenna, silence was never a sign of peace; it was a sign of calculation.
Valentina glanced sideways at her, noting the grim set of the warrior’s jaw. "You’ve gone quiet, Morwenna."
"That isn’t like you..."

"I’m thinking," Morwenna replied, her voice unnervingly steady despite the chaos. "I’m thinking about how many things in this city I believed to be absolute truths and how many of them died five minutes ago."
In the center of the hellscape, the fight had transcended human comprehension.
Xerollion had avoided Apollo’s devastating lunge by tilting his upper body precisely fifteen degrees. That was all.

His enhanced foresight had revealed the trajectory four seconds before Apollo had even fully committed to the motion, and his martial mastery had translated that data into the most economical correction possible: a minute shift of weight through his hips and a subtle rotation of his shoulders.
The blow, which carried enough kinetic force to level a fortress wall, whistled past his ear, close enough that the golden afterimage burned across his retinas like a brand.
Rex didn’t wait for the momentum to fade. He seized the opening with lethal intent.
WHAM!

He unleashed a straight kick, driving his boot upward with explosive force into Apollo’s midsection. It was a strike designed to shatter ribs and collapse lungs in a single heartbeat, the kind of blow that ended wars.
Apollo’s reflexes screamed. His forearm snapped up to intercept.
KRA KOOM!
The moment of impact was deafening. The life-affinity glow condensed along Apollo’s forearm like molten gold armor at the point of contact.
The kick, which should have folded him like parchment, instead drove him backward across the stone floor. His boots ground furrows into the rock as he skidded, sparks flying from the friction.
Just as he reached the limit of his slide, he planted his heel hard, absorbed the remaining kinetic energy through the reinforced tendons of his knee, and launched himself back into the fray.
Before the echo of Rex’s kick had even faded from the corridor, Apollo was already mid-assault, unleashing a lightning-fast four-punch combination that closed the distance with terrifying speed.
What followed stopped being a fight; it became a phenomenon.

For eleven seconds, the two combatants became a blur of impossible motion. To the soldiers thirty meters back, the exchange was less a series of blows and more a continuous strobing effect of gold and violet light.
Somewhere in that blur, forty individual strikes connected with bone-crushing force.
CRUNCH.
A sickening sound of cartilage grinding against cartilage echoed as Rex’s elbow struck Apollo’s ribs.
THUD CRACK.
Apollo’s fist connected with Rex’s ribs, sending a shockwave that shattered the nearby stone railing into shrapnel. Each connection produced its own localized pressure wave.
Men standing well outside the immediate radius felt the air slap against their faces in repeated, violent pulses, like standing too close to a series of explosions.

The corridor itself began to scream under the strain. Hairline cracks spiderwebbed across the ceiling and walls as the wild, uncontained magical discharge from blocked strikes found somewhere to vent.

High above, a massive stalactite the size of a supply cart snapped free from the ceiling forty meters behind them. It crashed to the floor with a thunderous explosion of stone and dust, but not a single soldier flinched.
Nobody moved.
Nobody breathed.
Every eye in the corridor was locked on the two monsters tearing each other apart in the center of the storm.

The blow, which carried enough kinetic force to level a fortress wall, whistled past his ear, close enough that the golden afterimage burned across his retinas like a brand.
Rex didn’t wait for the momentum to fade.
He seized the opening with lethal intent.
WHAM!
He unleashed a straight kick, driving his boot upward with explosive force into Apollo’s midsection.
It was a strike designed to shatter ribs and collapse lungs in a single heartbeat, the kind of blow that ended wars.
Apollo’s reflexes screamed.
His forearm snapped up to intercept.
KRA KOOM!
The moment of impact was deafening.
The life-affinity glow condensed along Apollo’s forearm like molten gold armor at the point of contact.
The kick, which should have folded him like parchment, instead drove him backward across the stone floor.
His boots ground furrows into the rock as he skidded, sparks flying from the friction.
Just as he reached the limit of his slide, he planted his heel hard, absorbed the remaining kinetic energy through the reinforced tendons of his knee, and launched himself back into the fray.
Before the echo of Rex’s kick had even faded from the corridor, Apollo was already mid-assault, unleashing a lightning-fast four-punch combination that closed the distance with terrifying speed.
What followed stopped being a fight; it became a phenomenon.
For eleven seconds, the two combatants became a blur of impossible motion.
To the soldiers thirty meters back, the exchange was less a series of blows and more a continuous strobing effect of gold and violet light.
Somewhere in that blur, forty individual strikes connected with bone-crushing force.
CRUNCH.
A sickening sound of cartilage grinding against cartilage echoed as Rex’s elbow struck Apollo’s ribs.
THUD CRACK.
Apollo’s fist connected with Rex’s ribs, sending a shockwave that shattered the nearby stone railing into shrapnel.
Each connection produced its own localized pressure wave.
Men standing well outside the immediate radius felt the air slap against their faces in repeated, violent pulses, like standing too close to a series of explosions.
The corridor itself began to scream under the strain.
Hairline cracks spiderwebbed across the ceiling and walls as the wild, uncontained magical discharge from blocked strikes found somewhere to vent.
High above, a massive stalactite the size of a supply cart snapped free from the ceiling forty meters behind them.
It crashed to the floor with a thunderous explosion of stone and dust, but not a single soldier flinched.
Nobody moved.
Nobody breathed.
Every eye in the corridor was locked on the two monsters tearing each other apart in the center of the storm.

chapters.title: Chapter 1150. So Why Does My Body Recognize His Rhythm?
paragraphs: The violence along the rest of the line did not cease all at once; it died by degrees, hemorrhaging momentum as the primal terror of the duel consumed everything else.

It began at the fringes nearest the epicenter. The soldiers there, demons who had been howling for blood, and Aethelgard spearmen who had been fighting for their lives found that their rage had simply evaporated.

Continuing to swing an axe at a comrade while a cataclysm was unfolding twenty meters away felt increasingly absurd, almost pathetic. Then, the stillness spread outward like a spreading rumor, a cold shiver running through the ranks.
Demon soldiers lowered their serrated blades. Aethelgard spearmen let their points drift toward the blood-slicked stone.
Within ninety seconds, the northern corridor, a space that had held the largest, most desperate engagement Erosyne had witnessed in four decades, had fallen into a deathly, ringing quiet.
The only sounds left were the wet thud of impacts, the grinding of bone, and the explosive tearing sounds that each collision ripped from the air.
Without a single command being issued, a boundary formed.

The soldiers of both armies, enemies who moments ago would have killed each other without hesitation, simply backed away from the center. They retreated in a synchronized, instinctual withdrawal until a rough circle of open ground had formed around the duel, creating a makeshift arena of devastation.
Then, because armies are made of frightened, desperate people who cannot witness something this transcendent in silence for long, the noise began.
"APOLLO!"
The chant erupted like a controlled explosion somewhere in the Aethelgard third rank. Within seconds, it tore through the entire formation.
Thousands of voices hammered the name into the stone walls, each syllable vibrating in the lungs of every soldier present.

Men who had been retreating in genuine, soul-crushing panic ten minutes earlier were now pressed against the invisible boundary of the fight, their faces streaked with blood and tears, fists pumping the air in a desperate bid to give their champion strength.
"APOLLO! APOLLO! APOLLO!"
The response from the opposing side came not as a shout, but as something darker, a low, guttural rumble that shook the floorboards of reality.
THOOM. THOOM. THOOM.

Orcs began beating their weapon hafts against the corridor floor in a slow, building rhythm that sounded like the heartbeat of a dying god. Demons roared a name that most Aethelgard soldiers had only heard in nightmares less than an hour ago.
The sound was alien, terrifying, and utterly devoted.

Cassandra stood at the very front of the demonic line. Her arms were folded across her chest, her transformation still burning like banked embers, a dark, crimson aura that writhed around her shoulders like living smoke.
She did not join the chanting. She simply watched, her lips pressed into a thin line, but the expression on her face carried something dangerously close to pride.
She watched her chosen instrument tear through the world.
Beside her, Gorvasha stood like a statue carved from granite, her massive warhammer planted head down on the stone.

She watched the duel with the grim, terrifying satisfaction of a commander whose faith in her leader had not just been met but had been violently, publicly validated in front of every soldier under her command.
In the center of the circle, the two combatants ignored the thousands of screaming voices.
To them, there was no army. There was no war.
There was only the taste of copper in their mouths, the searing pain of cracked ribs, and the endless, beautiful cycle of violence between them.

Elliot Von Starlight stood at the precipice of the Aethelgard crowd, his body coiled like a spring under immense tension. His hands were clenched into fists so tight that his knuckles had gone bloodless and white, the tendons in his forearms standing out like steel cables.
His mind was a storm of memories. He had fought shoulder to shoulder with Apollo since they were sixteen-year-old novices.
He had been there when Apollo had stood alone against a rampaging rank three drake during their third year at the Academy, blood streaming down his face as he claimed victory.
On more than one occasion, in the quiet hours between training sessions, Elliot had privately believed that his friend was the apex, the strongest combatant their generation would ever produce.

And now, he was watching that apex being systematically dismantled. He was watching Apollo get outclassed by a shadow, a masked figure who had not yet shown even the slightest sign of exhaustion or strain.
"I should be in there," Elliot rasped, his voice cracking with raw desperation. "I can’t just stand here while he gets slaughtered."
"You shouldn’t." Evelyn’s hand clamped around his forearm like a vice, anchoring him to the spot.
Her grip was painful, but he barely noticed.
"Evelyn, look at him!" Elliot turned to her, his eyes wild with panic. "He’s losing... He’s being broken apart right in front of us!"
"He’s not losing yet," she said, though her voice lacked its usual conviction. "And if you rush in there, you won’t just die... you’ll die in approximately four seconds!"
"And then Apollo will have to watch his friend die while he’s already fighting for his own life!"
"Do you want that burden on him?!"
She didn’t look at him. Her gaze remained locked on the masked figure, her pupils dilated, her eyes narrowing into something hard, analytical, and deeply unhappy.
"There’s something wrong with this, Elliot. Something fundamentally wrong."
"There’s a lot wrong," he spat, glancing back at the dust clouds and the flashes of light. "The power levels alone are insane.
"No." She shook her head slowly, a frown deepening between her brows. "Not the power."
"The power is something alien, something I don’t recognize... It’s the geometry of it. The way he moves, I’ve seen it before."
Elliot blinked, momentarily distracted from his own terror. "What are you talking about?"
"The way he shifts his weight a microsecond before he commits a strike..."

"The way he rotates his hips to absorb momentum... that specific, lethal timing on the counterattack." Her voice dropped to a whisper, laced with genuine unease. "I’ve seen someone move like that, and I cannot place where, and it is driving me insane."
"You think you know him?" Elliot asked, a cold dread pooling in his stomach.
Evelyn finally tore her eyes away from the carnage to look at him properly. Her face was pale.
"I think I’ve watched him fight before... And that should be impossible, because until sixty minutes ago, nobody in Aethelgard had ever seen this man’s face, heard his name, or witnessed his style."
"So why does my body recognize his rhythm?"
Ten meters away, embedded within the front ranks of the Aethelgard soldiers who were pressed against the edge of the killing circle, Rex Rexilion stood in deceptive stillness.
His face was a masterpiece of deception; he wore an expression of tightly controlled alarm that would have convinced any veteran soldier that he was witnessing a tragedy.

’I have to change the flow,’ Rex thought, his inner mind cold and calculating even as his pulse remained steady. ’I need to break their concentration, break his rhythm, and give myself the opening to end this without suspicion.’

He took two deliberate steps forward, breaking past the front line. Two soldiers instinctively reached out, their hands grasping at his cloak to pull him back from the invisible boundary of the duel. Rex ignored them, cupping a hand beside his mouth.
"APOLLO!" The shout tore across the open ground, carrying the perfect, jagged edge of genuine terror. "APOLLO, LOOK OUT!"
"LET ME HELP YOU!"

The lie landed like a stone in a still pond. He took another step forward, his body angled toward the fight, his weight shifting onto his front foot in the precise, heroic posture of a man about to commit himself to a suicidal rescue.
To every soldier watching, he looked like a hero willing to throw his life away for a brother in arms.
"Stay back, soldier!" a Nightwing captain roared, recognizing the breach of protocol.
Three more soldiers grabbed Rex’s shoulders, physically hauling him back into formation, their faces grim with the belief that they were saving a brave man from a mad death.
Rex allowed himself to be pulled back, his eyes never leaving Apollo’s back. Beneath the mask, his lips curled into something predatory.
The stage was set.
